title: Chapter 3: Vectors
text:
Overview
Up to this point, you have been writing code in the Console and saving your work in R Scripts. In this chapter, you begin working in an R Notebook (.Rmd). An R Notebook keeps your writing and code together and lets you view the output alongside them. This record helps another person, or your future self, follow, check, and rerun your work.
You will practice transparency by writing short memos near your code. These memos explain your goal, what the code does, what the output shows, what you checked, and what you are still working to understand. The notebook becomes a record of both your analysis and your learning.
The coding focus is vectors. You will build numeric vectors, perform vectorized arithmetic, create sequences, and work with exponents. You will then examine how mode(), typeof(), and class() describe R objects. Dates, character vectors, factors, and coercion show how an object’s type and class affect the way R stores, prints, and works with its values.
By the end of the chapter, you should be able to create and rerun an R Notebook, document your work with short memos, work with several kinds of vectors, and use checks to explain how R is storing and interpreting your objects.
In this chapter, you will learn how to:

title: Chapter 3: Vectors
text:
📝 Create, rename, and save an R Notebook (.Rmd).
📍 Run R code from code chunks.
✍️ Practice transparency with 🗣 Comment, 🪞 Reflect, and 👀 Cite memos that make your code, output, checks, learning, and resource use visible.
🛠 Build numeric vectors with c() and check them with length().
🧮 Use arithmetic operators, sequences, and exponents with numeric vectors.
📈 Explain vectorization and recognize when R recycles a shorter vector.
🔎 Use mode(), typeof(), and class() to inspect how R stores and interprets objects.
🔤 Create and combine character vectors.
🏷️ Create factors and inspect their levels.
🔄 Explain coercion and use conversion functions to change an object’s type.
🧹 Clear your Environment, run your notebook from top to bottom, and knit it to HTML to verify that the notebook works in order.

title: Chapter 3: Vectors
text:
R Notebooks—Part 1
An R Notebook is an R Markdown (.Rmd) document that combines Markdown writing with R code organized in code chunks. You can run the code interactively and keep your code, output, and explanatory text together in one document.
The utility is reproducible thinking: your code, your results, and your memo-style notes live in one place, in order, so someone else (including future-you) can follow what happened.
R Notebooks are similar to R Scripts but offer additional features such as:

Interactive Code Execution: You can run individual lines, selected lines, or complete code chunks.
Rich Text Formatting: You can use Markdown to format text, add headings, lists, links, and images.
Output Display: Depending on your RStudio settings, output can appear below the chunk or in the Console, Plots, Viewer, or another relevant pane.
Reproducibility: R Notebooks support reproducible research by allowing you to combine code and narrative in a single document.


R Script vs R Notebook
An R Notebook provides more room for memoing than an R Script. A script can hold code and short # comments. An R Notebook also allows full Markdown memos between code chunks. This supports an inspectable and reproducible workflow.








Feature
R Script
R Notebook




File Extension
.R
.Rmd


Code Execution
Run individual lines, selected lines, or the entire script
Run individual lines, selected lines, or complete chunks


Output Display
Console, Plots, Viewer, or another relevant RStudio pane
Below code chunks or in another RStudio pane, depending on settings


Explanatory Writing
# comments inside the script
Markdown prose between chunks and # comments inside chunks


Memoing
Short comments placed near code
Formatted memos placed alongside code and output





Open a New R Notebook
To open an R Notebook, you will need to install the rmarkdown package and then create a new R Notebook file in RStudio.

Step 0: Install the rmarkdown package
To use R Notebooks, you need the rmarkdown package and then create a new R Notebook file in RStudio. A package is an installable bundle of tools—functions, documentation, and sometimes data—that extends what R can do. Most packages are downloaded from CRAN (the main public repository for R packages).
Method A. Packages Tab

In RStudio, go to the Packages tab in the bottom-right pane. It is in the same area as the Files tab.
Click on 📥 Install.
In the dialog box that appears, type rmarkdown in the Packages field.
Make sure Install dependencies is checked.
Click Install.

✅ Check: If installation succeeds, you should see messages in the Console showing what was installed.
Method B. Console Pane

In RStudio, go to the Console pane (bottom-left).
Type the following command and press Enter:


install.packages("rmarkdown")


# After installation, confirm that rmarkdown is installed:
packageVersion("rmarkdown")


🧐 Notice: install.packages() is a setup command. Run it in the Console when the package is not installed. Do not add it to code that runs whenever the notebook runs.


# install.packages("rmarkdown")



Step 1: Open an R Notebook
To create an R Notebook in RStudio:

Go to File > New File > R Notebook.
An .Rmd file opens in the Source pane.

💡 Tip: If your RStudio version does not show “R Notebook,” choose R Markdown. Select HTML Notebook as the output format. The end result is still an R Notebook stored as an .Rmd file.



The YAML Header
At the very top of your notebook you will see a block that looks like this:
---
title: "Untitled"
output: html_notebook
---
This is called the YAML header (pronounced “YAM-ul”). It is document metadata—settings that control the notebook’s title and output type. Think of it as the document’s “front label,” not code.

Renaming the Notebook
🎯 Edit the title so it describes the work in this notebook.
---
title: "Chapter 3 Guided Activity"
output: html_notebook
---


Saving the Notebook
🎯 To save your R Notebook:

Go to File > Save As....
Choose a folder where you keep your R work (e.g., Data-R155).
Name the file chapter3_notes.
Note that the file extension is .Rmd.

✅ Check: Confirm that chapter3_notes.Rmd appears in the Files pane.



Code Chunks
A code chunk is a fenced block where R code runs. It begins with three backticks plus {r} and ends with three backticks: ```{r} … ```.
```{r}
# your R code
```
Code chunks are the sections of an R Notebook that contain runnable R code. Put R code inside a chunk. When you run the chunk, RStudio displays the result in the notebook or in another relevant pane, depending on your output settings.
Memos are the notes you write to explain your code and results. In an R Notebook, write memos as regular text between code chunks, without needing to comment them out with #. This allows you to keep your code, results, and memos together in one document.

Inserting Code Chunks
Method A. Toolbar Button
Click the Insert Chunk button in the toolbar and choose R from the drop-down list.
In RStudio, the insert chunk button usually looks like a green button with a C or an icon depending on version.



R Notebook Toolbar with Insert Chunk Button Highlighted


Method B. Keyboard Shortcut
Press Ctrl + Alt + I (Windows/Linux) or Cmd + Option + I (macOS).
Method C. Manually Type
Type the following lines in your R Notebook:
```{r}
# your R code
```
💡 Tip: Remember that these are backticks and not single quotes. The backtick is located on the same key as the tilde (~) on most keyboards, just above the tab button.



Run Code Chunks
Like so many things in R, there are several ways you can run code chunks.
Method A. Run Menu
Click the Run menu at the top of RStudio and select Run Current Chunk or Run All Chunks.



R Notebook Code Chunk with Run Button Highlighted


Method B. Play Button
Click the green play button (▶) at the top-right of the chunk.



R Notebook Code Chunk play button


Method C. Keyboard Shortcut
Place your cursor inside the chunk and press Ctrl + Shift + Enter (Windows/Linux) or Cmd + Shift + Enter (macOS).

Example: Vector Arithmetic
Vectorization allows an operation to work directly with a vector instead of requiring you to process one element at a time. In the arithmetic examples below, R applies the operation element by element.
🎯 Insert a code chunk then type and run the following R code to do vector arithmetic.
```{r}

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
x <- c(2, 4, 6)
y <- c(1, 3, 5)

x + y     # We should see three values: 3, 7, and 11

```
🎯 Click the green play button in the chunk (top-right of the chunk), or use the Run menu to run the current chunk / all chunks.
[1]  3  7 11
🗣 Modeled Comment: The output shows the result of adding the two vectors element by element: 2 + 1 = 3, 4 + 3 = 7, and 6 + 5 = 11.
```{r}

#  ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
x * 2
x / y

```
[1]  4  8 12
[1] 2.000000 1.333333 1.200000
🗣 Modeled Comment: The code chunk contains two calculations, and the results appear in the same order as the calculations.
🎯 Try creating a sequence of powers of 3 using the exponent operator ^. Create a vector named small_exponents that contains the integers from 0 to 4, then create a new vector named powers_of_three that raises 3 to the power of each element in small_exponents.
```{r}

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
small_exponents <- 0:4
powers_of_three <- 3 ^ small_exponents

powers_of_three

[1]  1  3  9 27 81


```
```{r}

length(powers_of_three)

[1] 5


```
🗣 Modeled Comment: R reads 3 ^ small_exponents as “raise 3 to each value stored in small_exponents.” The vector small_exponents tells R which exponents to use. The length tells us how many powers were created, not how large the biggest value is.
✍️ Transparency: Keep a visible record of your learning as you work. The examples below model 🗣 Comment, 🪞 Reflect, and 👀 Cite memos in Markdown outside code chunks.

title: Chapter 3: Vectors
text:
Memoing in R Notebooks
The code chunk is like a mini R Script. Inside a code chunk, memo text must start with # or R will try to run it as code (and may error). Treat # like a “do not execute” marker for the computer.

🧐 Notice: Text outside code chunks does not have # because it is regular paragraph writing. R will not try to run it as code.

A 🗣 Comment prompt asks for a Markdown memo outside the code chunk unless the instructions say otherwise. This differs from an R code comment, which begins with # inside a chunk.
Markdown lets you write memos as readable paragraphs instead of a wall of # comments. Markdown is a simple formatting syntax for creating headings, lists, links, and other structured text. In R Notebooks, you can write Markdown text between code chunks to explain your thought process, document your findings, and provide context for your code.
Click on a blank line outside the chunk and type a short memo like this:
✍️ Transparency memo

🎯 Goal: Practice creating vectors and doing arithmetic.
✅ Check: I should see three outputs: x + y, x * 2, and x / y.
🗣 Comment: The three outputs each contain one result for every position in x. R added x and y element by element, multiplied each value in x by 2, and divided each value in x by the matching value in y.
🪞 Reflect: I initially expected x + y to produce one total. Seeing three values helped me understand that vector arithmetic works position by position.

If a resource helped you understand or troubleshoot the example, add a 👀 Cite memo that identifies the resource and explains what it contributed.

💬 What does this look like in practice?
✍️ Transparency Memo Example



R Notebook showing arithmetic code with commented-out error lines, pasted console errors (“unexpected ‘,’” and “object not found”), memos identifying the typo, missing object, and case sensitivity, and corrected code printing the ratio.



🧐 Notice: This is a ✍️ transparent record because the student kept the unsuccessful code and error messages visible, wrote memos explaining what caused the errors, revised the code, used ✅ Check to run the corrected code, and added a 🗣 Comment explaining the final result.


Now that you can write code in code chunks and memos in regular text, practice recycling vectors while keeping a transparent research journal.

Example: Recycling Vectors
When you perform arithmetic on two vectors of different lengths, R will recycle the shorter one to match the longer one.
🎯 Create a new vector named recycled_result by adding the combination vector to the numbers3 vector.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
numbers3 <- c(1.5, 2.5, -3.5)     # length of 3 elements
combination <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)   # length of 5 elements
recycled_result <- numbers3 + combination

Warning in numbers3 + combination: longer object length is not a multiple of
shorter object length


⚠️ A Warning message appears because the longer vector length is not a multiple of the shorter vector length. R still completes the calculation by recycling the shorter vector, but the warning tells you to stop and verify that both vector lengths are what you intended.
```{r}

# ✅ Check the recycled_result vector
print(recycled_result)

```
[1]  2.5  4.5 -0.5  5.5  7.5
🗣 Modeled Comment: R recycles numbers3 by repeating it as needed: 1.5, 2.5, -3.5, 1.5, 2.5. Then R adds element-by-element: 1 + 1.5, 2 + 2.5, 3 + -3.5, 4 + 1.5, and 5 + 2.5.

✍️ Transparency Memo Example



R Notebook chunk subtracting vectors of different lengths, output showing the recycled subtraction results, and a memo explaining that R repeats the shorter vector to match the longer one (with the AI tool credited).



🧐 Notice: The student used 🪞 Reflect to identify what was confusing, used 👀 Cite to name ChatGPT and explain how it helped, and then added a 🗣 Comment explaining in her own words how R recycled the shorter vector.



Next, examine how R describes an object’s underlying storage and how its class affects the way R prints and works with it.

title: Chapter 3: Vectors
text:
Vector Types and Classes
In this section you will learn how class affects how R interprets an object and decides how it should behave.

Class and Behavior
Recall from Chapter 2 that an atomic vector contains elements of one underlying type. R can describe an object at different levels. typeof() reports its specific internal storage type, mode() reports a broader storage category, and class() reports how R interprets the object and selects methods for it. Some objects, such as dates and factors, have a class that adds meaning to their underlying storage.
For example, an object created with as.Date() has class "Date", underlying type "double", and mode "numeric". The "Date" class tells R to print and work with the object as a date.
🎯 Store any date in a variable named start_date using as.Date(). Then use mode(), typeof(), and class() to compare the underlying storage with the way R treats the object.
```{r}

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
start_date <- as.Date("2026-08-24")
print(start_date)

```
```{r}

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
mode(start_date)
typeof(start_date)
class(start_date)

```
🗣 Modeled Comment: mode(start_date) returns "numeric", typeof(start_date) returns "double", and class(start_date) returns "Date". The class tells R to print and work with the object as a date.
Why does this matter? R uses the "Date" class to apply date-specific behavior even though the object is stored underneath as a double.
🎯 What date was it one week after start_date?
```{r}

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
start_date + 7

```
🗣 Modeled Comment: R treats 7 as seven days and returns the date one week after start_date.


Types, Modes, and Classes
Every object has an underlying type. typeof() reports the specific internal storage type. mode() reports a broader storage category. For example, integer and double vectors both have mode "numeric".
class() reports how R should interpret an object. For an ordinary double vector, typeof() returns "double" while class() returns "numeric". For an object with a special class, such as a date or factor, the class adds meaning and affects how functions print and work with it.
Common Atomic Vector Types:

double: numbers such as 1 and 3.14
integer: whole numbers explicitly marked with L, such as 1L and 2L
character: text strings such as "Hello World" and "R is fun"
logical: TRUE, FALSE, or NA
complex: complex numbers such as 1 + 2i

Classes Used in This Chapter:

Date: a class for dates, usually built on double storage, such as as.Date("2026-01-01")
factor: a class for categorical data, built on integer codes and a set of category labels called levels



Character Strings
A character string is a sequence of characters enclosed in quotes. Character strings are used to represent text data in R.
The paste() function in R is used to concatenate (combine) strings together. It takes multiple string arguments and combines them into a single string, with an optional separator between them.

✍️ Transparency Memo Example



R Notebook using paste() to combine “yellow” and “banana” into “yellow banana,” then class(sentence) returning “character,” followed by a memo noting confusion about what “character” means.



🧐 Notice: The student used 🪞 Reflect to record an unexpected result and a specific question about the word "character". A useful next step would be to review the chapter, ask a peer or instructor, or consult another resource allowed for the work. If a resource helps, use 👀 Cite to identify it and explain what it contributed.


paste() works across vectors too, combining elements element-wise.
🎯 Create two character vectors named first_names and last_names, then use the paste() function to combine them into a new vector named full_names.
```{r}

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
first_names <- c("Demi", "Snoop", "Ed")
last_names <- c("Moore", "Dogg", "Sheeran")
full_names <- paste(first_names, last_names)

```
```{r}

# ✅ Check the full_names vector
print(full_names)

```
🗣 Modeled Comment: The output shows the full names created by combining the first and last names element-wise.
🌳 If you don’t want spaces, try paste0(first_names, last_names).


Factor Vectors (Categorical Data)
A factor is R’s way of storing categorical data. Factors store values that come from a fixed set of categories, such as “freshman,” “sophomore,” “junior,” and “senior.” Factors are common in data analysis because they help R treat categories correctly in tables, summaries, and models.
A factor often prints labels that look like character values, but its internal storage and class are different. R stores a standard factor using integer codes and uses its levels to connect those codes with category labels.

Creating Factors
The function factor() creates a factor from a vector. Character input is common because the vector values become category labels.
📜 The SYNTAX (basic):
factor(x)
Here, x is the vector you want to convert into a factor.
🎯 Create a factor vector named grades that contains the following letter grades: “A”, “B”, “C”, “A”, “B”, “A” using the factor() function.
```{r}

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
grades <- c("A", "B", "C", "A", "B", "A")
grades <- factor(grades)

```
🗣 Modeled Comment: The object grades is overwritten as a factor using the factor() function because the same name is used in the assignment process grades <-.
```{r}

# ✅ Check the grades factor
mode(grades)
typeof(grades)
class(grades)
print(grades)

```
[1] "numeric"
[1] "integer"
[1] "factor"
[1] A B C A B A
Levels: A B C
🗣 Modeled Comment: The output shows that the grades object has class "factor". Underneath, R stores the factor using integer codes, even though it prints the category labels.


Levels and Ordering
The printed output above displays the levels of the factor. Levels are the possible category labels a factor can contain. A factor can retain a level even when no current element uses it. Unless you specify levels, R generally creates levels from the observed values and orders character labels alphabetically.
Even though factors print category labels, R stores a standard factor underneath as integer codes. typeof() reports the internal type as "integer", mode() reports the broader mode as "numeric", and class() reports "factor". You can control the possible categories and their order by supplying the levels argument when creating the factor.
🎯 Create a factor vector named sizes with levels ordered as "Small", "Medium", and "Large" using the factor() function.
```{r}

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
sizes <- c("Medium", "Large", "Small", "Medium", "Large")
sizes <- factor(sizes, levels = c("Small", "Medium", "Large"))

```
```{r}

# ✅ Check the sizes factor
print(sizes)

```
🗣 Modeled Comment: The output shows the sizes factor with levels ordered as "Small", "Medium", and "Large", as specified in the factor() function.

✍️ Transparency Memo Example



R Notebook creating a character vector of class standings, converting it to a factor, and showing levels() plus mode()/typeof() outputs; memo questions why the factor prints words but stores integer codes, with a follow-up memo summarizing the explanation (integer codes + levels labels).



🧐 Notice: This is a ✍️ transparent record because the student used ✅ Check to compare class, mode, type, and levels; used 🪞 Reflect to record the contradiction between integer storage and printed words; and used 👀 Cite to identify ChatGPT and summarize what it contributed to the final understanding.

This is a high-quality memo because it captures confusion, gathers diagnostic evidence, and then resolves the confusion with a correct explanation.

Next, examine what happens when values of different types are combined in one atomic vector.



Data Coercion
An atomic vector stores elements of one type. If you try to mix types, R will coerce (convert) them to a common type based on a hierarchy of flexibility.
🎯 What happens if you mix numbers and characters?
```{r}

mixed <- c("candy", 4, "book", 92)

# ✅ Check the mixed vector
print(mixed)
class(mixed)

```
🗣 Modeled Comment: The values 4 and 92 print as character values because the entire vector was coerced to character.
An atomic vector stores elements of one underlying type. Mixing types triggers coercion to a common type. A common coercion order is logical → integer → double → complex → character. R moves toward a type that can represent all the elements.

Converting Between Types
You can explicitly convert between types using functions like as.numeric(), as.character(), and as.logical().
The as.numeric() function tries to convert characters to numbers. If it can’t, it returns NA (not available).
📜 The SYNTAX (basic):
as.numeric(x)
🎯 Try converting a character vector of numbers to numeric using the as.numeric() function.
```{r}

as.numeric(c("1", "2", "3")) # character → numeric: text converts to numbers

```
🗣 Modeled Comment: The output shows the numeric values 1, 2, and 3 successfully converted from character strings.
🎯 Try converting the mixed vector to numeric using the as.numeric() function.
```{r}

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
as.numeric(mixed)            # character → numeric: text converts to NA

```
🗣 Modeled Comment: The output shows NA for "candy" and "book" because those text values cannot be converted to numbers. The character values "4" and "92" can be converted to numeric values, so they become 4 and 92.
R also gives the warning NAs introduced by coercion because some character values could not be converted to numbers. The warning tells you to inspect the new NA values and determine which conversions failed.

text:
Summary
In this chapter, you began using an R Notebook to keep writing, code, and output in one inspectable workflow. You practiced transparency by adding short memos that record what your code does, what the output shows, what you checked, and what you learned.
You created numeric vectors with c(), checked their length, used arithmetic operators, built sequences with : and seq(), and applied exponents. You also examined vectorization and recycling, including the warning R gives when vector lengths do not align evenly.
You then used mode(), typeof(), and class() to investigate how R stores and interprets objects. Dates, character vectors, factors, levels, and coercion demonstrated how underlying type and class affect behavior. You finished by clearing the Environment, running the notebook from top to bottom, and knitting it to HTML to verify that the record works in order.

title: Chapter 3: Vectors
text:
Chapter Terms
Backtick: The ` character (above the Tab key) used for code-related formatting and quoting. In Markdown, single backticks mark inline code and triple backticks create fenced code blocks; in R Markdown, backticks also mark inline R code (`r …`), including inside YAML fields like date: “`r Sys.Date()`”, which gets evaluated when you render the document. In R, backticks can also quote non-syntactic names (e.g., names with spaces) so they can be used safely in code.
Coercion: The process by which R converts values of different types to a common type when they are combined in a vector. For example, if you combine numbers and characters, R will coerce the numbers to characters.
Character String: A single piece of text in R, stored as a character value and written in quotes (for example, “My favorite color is yellow!” or “Who stole the cookie from the cookie jar?”).
Class class(): A function that reports the object’s class, which tells R how to interpret the object and which methods to use when functions are applied to it. For example, class(3.14) returns "numeric", and class(mtcars) returns "data.frame".
Code Chunks: Fenced blocks in an R Markdown or Quarto document that contain executable code, usually beginning with ```{r} and ending with three backticks. Code can be run interactively or during rendering. Depending on RStudio settings, output may appear below the chunk or in another relevant pane.
Factor Class: An R object class for categorical data, where each value is stored as an integer code that points to a category label. Factors help R handle categories correctly in tables, plots, and statistical models, even though they may print like text.
Factor Levels: The distinct category labels a factor can take (for example, "freshman", "sophomore", "junior", "senior"). Levels define the set and order of categories, and each factor value is internally stored as the index of its level.
Markdown: A lightweight plain-text formatting syntax used to write structured documents (headings, lists, links, emphasis, code) in a way that stays readable as plain text and can be rendered into formats like HTML on many platforms and tools.
NA: A special constant that marks a missing value (“Not Available”)—meaning the data point is unknown or not recorded. R also provides typed missing values like NA_integer_, NA_real_, NA_character_, and NA_complex_ to match the underlying data type.
Object Name: The variable name you assign with <- that refers to the entire object in your environment. You use the object name to print, modify, or pass the whole object to functions.
Package: An installable collection of R code—functions, documentation, and sometimes datasets—that adds new features beyond base R. Packages are commonly installed from CRAN and then loaded with library() so you can use their tools in your session.
R Markdown: A document format (.Rmd) that mixes plain-text writing (Markdown) with embedded R code chunks, so you can generate reports that combine narrative, code, and computed output. You can render an R Markdown file into finished formats like HTML, PDF, or Word.
R Notebook: An .Rmd document that combines Markdown writing with R code chunks. You can run code interactively and view results below chunks or in another relevant pane, depending on your RStudio settings. Rendering creates a finished document that combines narrative, code, and computed output.
Recycling: R’s rule for handling vector operations when vectors have different lengths. R repeats the shorter vector as needed and then performs the operation element by element. If the longer length is not an exact multiple of the shorter length, R issues a warning. If it is an exact multiple, recycling occurs silently, so you should still verify that recycling was intentional.
Research Journal: A running record of your analysis and learning process. This includes the questions you asked, code you tried, outputs you received, resources you consulted, and decisions you made. In practice, you can maintain this record in an R Script or R Notebook using notes, comments, checks, and citations.
Transparency: The practice of disclosing the methods, materials, assumptions, values, and interests that shaped the work. In an R Notebook, transparency means keeping relevant code, output, decisions, checks, and resource use visible so the process can be examined.
Vector: A fundamental R data structure. Atomic vectors store elements of one underlying type, while lists can contain elements of different types and lengths. In this chapter, vector refers primarily to atomic vectors created with functions such as c().
Vector Arithmetic: Performing mathematical operations directly on vectors. In R, operations such as +, -, *, /, and ^ are applied element by element, so c(1, 2, 3) + c(10, 20, 30) returns c(11, 22, 33).
Vectorization: Writing an operation so it works directly with a vector instead of processing one element at a time in an explicit loop. In element-wise operations, R pairs corresponding elements and returns a vector of results. Other vectorized functions may summarize or otherwise transform the complete vector.
Warning: A console message indicating that R did run the command but detected a potential problem. Execution continues and a result is produced, but the output may be incomplete, unexpected, or based on an assumption (for example, coercing types, removing missing elements, or using a function in a way that may not behave as intended).
YAML Header: The metadata section at the top of an R Markdown or Quarto document, written between --- lines, that controls document settings like the title, author, date, output format (HTML/PDF/Word), and options for rendering.

📝 Practice Space
Fill in the blanks to complete the code in your R Notebook.
Before you begin:

Create a new R Notebook in RStudio.
Save it in the folder where you keep your Intro to R work as chapter3_practice.Rmd.
Complete all Practice Space tasks in that notebook.
Save your workspace as chapter3_practice.RData where you keep your Intro to R work.

✍️ Transparency: Write your memo responses as Markdown text outside the code chunks. Keep them near the code and output they explain.

🗣 Comment: Explain what the code, output, evidence, or decision means.
🪞 Reflect: Record what you learned, what confused you, what changed in your understanding, or what you would do next.
👀 Cite: If you use help from a peer, instructor, documentation, website, or AI tool, identify the resource and explain what it contributed. Follow the policies that apply to your work.

Keep each memo focused. One to three thoughtful sentences is enough. Complete each 🗣 Comment prompt and the 🪞 Reflect prompts included with selected tasks.
If you encounter an error, practice tenacity by choosing an informed next step and transparency by recording what happened, what you tried, what you checked, and what remains unclear. If a resource helped you troubleshoot, include a 👀 Cite memo near that work.
Before you finish, clear your Environment and run the notebook from top to bottom. Then knit to HTML to check that the notebook works in order.

Task 1
🛠 Build numeric vectors
🎯 Build two numeric vectors where both vectors are the same length.

Create a vector called sales_q1 with FOUR numbers of your choice values.


# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook, Fill in the blanks
sales_q1 <- c(___, ___, ___, ___)


Create a vector called sales_q2 with FOUR numbers of your choice values.


# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook, Fill in the blanks
sales_q2 <- c(___, ___, ___, ___)


# ✅ Check the sales_q1 and sales_q2
print(___)
___(sales_q2)

length(___)
___(sales_q2)

🗣 Comment: In 1–3 sentences, explain what print() and length() show for sales_q1 and sales_q2. State how you verified that the vectors have the same length.


Task 2
📈 Vector arithmetic
Using vector arithmetic, create an object named growth that stores the difference between sales_q2 and sales_q1.
💡 Tip: One of the missing characters is an operator.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook, Fill in the blanks
growth <- ______ _ ______


# ✅ Check the growth vector
print(growth)

🗣 Comment: In 1–3 sentences, explain what each value in growth represents and how it was calculated from sales_q1 and sales_q2.


Task 3
🔢 Exponents and vectorized math
🎯 Create a numeric vector named binary_powers that contains the powers of 2 from (2^0) through (2^{10}).
First, create a vector that stores the exponent values. Then use that vector on the right side of the ^ operator. 💡 Tip: Do not build the exponent vector out of powers. The exponents vector will store the exponent positions.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook, Fill in the blanks

# Step 1: create the exponent values 0 through 10
exponents <- 0:10

# Step 2: raise the base to each exponent value
binary_powers <- 2 ___ exponents


# ✅ Check the length of the binary_powers vector
_____(binary_powers)
print(binary_powers)

🗣 Comment: In 1–3 sentences, explain what length(binary_powers) and print(binary_powers) show. Include how many values are in the vector and why the first value is 1.
🪞 Reflect: Before running the code, did you expect 2 ^ exponents to create one answer or many answers? In 1–3 sentences, explain how this task changed or confirmed your understanding of vectorized math in R.


Task 4
📈 Subtract one vector from another
🎯 Find the anomaly by subtracting the cursed_seq vector from the travel_jumps vector. We’ll recreate vectors seen in Chapter 2 and then subtract them.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
cursed_seq <- c(4L, 8L, 15L, 16L, 23L, 42L)          # Integer via c()


# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
travel_jumps <- seq(from = 1887, to = 2052, by = 33)   # numeric via seq()


# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook, Fill in the blanks
anomaly <- __________ - __________


# ✅ Check the anomaly vector
print(anomaly)

🗣 Comment: In 1–3 sentences, explain how R produced the values in anomaly by pairing travel_jumps with cursed_seq.
These are just playful example vectors. The important skill is subtracting one vector from another.


Task 5
🔎 Check type and class
A class tells R how to interpret an object and how functions should treat it. The mode() and typeof() functions help you inspect what kind of data R is storing.
🎯 Use mode(), typeof(), and class() to inspect different R objects.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
lucky_numbers <- c(3, 7, 11, 42)

values <- c("curious", "careful", "honest", "open")


# ✅ Check lucky_numbers
mode(__________)
typeof(__________)
class(__________)


# ✅ Check values
mode(__________)
typeof(__________)
class(__________)

🗣 Comment: In 1–3 sentences, explain what mode(), typeof(), and class() showed for lucky_numbers and values.
🪞 Reflect: Did R treat the number vector and the word vector the same way or differently? In 1–3 sentences, explain what this helped you notice about how R stores objects.


Task 6
🏷️ Create and check a factor
A factor helps R treat values as categories instead of ordinary text. Factor levels are the allowed category labels stored inside a factor.
🎯 Create a factor for categorical data, then inspect its class and levels.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook. Fill in the blank.
course_path <- c("Core", "Advanced", "Core", "Core", "Advanced", "Core")

course_path_factor <- ______(course_path)


# ✅ Check the factor
class(__________________)
levels(__________________)
print(__________________)

🗣 Comment: In 1–3 sentences, explain what class(course_path_factor) and levels(course_path_factor) show.
🪞 Reflect: Why might R need a special class for categorical values instead of treating everything as ordinary character text? Keep your answer to 1–3 sentences.


Task 7
🪞 Reflect on coercion
A single atomic vector can only store one basic data type at a time. When numbers and text are mixed in the same vector, R has to choose one type that can hold all the values. This process is called coercion.
🎯 Explain why numeric values may be coerced to character values if you mix them inside a single vector.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
mixed_vector <- c(10, 20, "thirty", 40)


# ✅ Check whether coercion happened
print(mixed_vector)
mode(mixed_vector)
typeof(mixed_vector)
class(mixed_vector)

🗣 Comment: In 1–3 sentences, explain why R turns the numeric values into character values when numbers and text are combined in one atomic vector.
✅ Check: Name one function or output you would use to confirm that coercion happened.
🪞 Reflect: In 1–3 sentences, explain what this task clarified or changed in your understanding of how an atomic vector stores mixed values.


Task 8
✅ Final checks
🎯 Step 1: Sweep your Environment. Start clean.
Click the 🧹 broom icon in the Environment pane to clear objects.
🎯 Step 2: Run everything top-to-bottom.
Use Run → Run All to execute every chunk in order. If an error appears, document what happened, what you tried, and how you resolved it or what still confuses you.
🎯 Step 3: Knit to HTML.
Knit your notebook to HTML to check that the report works from beginning to end.
🎯 Step 4: Save your work.
After your notebook runs without errors, save the .Rmd file and review the rendered HTML.

title: Chapter 4: Structures
text:
Overview
Chapter 3 introduced R Notebook memos as a way to keep your code, output, checks, and learning visible. In this chapter, you will apply transparency while deciding which vector values to select and filter.
Your memos will record what you intended to select, which indexing method you used, how you checked the result, and what the output showed. This creates a record that you and another reader can follow later.
This chapter also finishes the vector-selection skills you need before working with larger datasets. You will learn how vector elements can be labeled with names, how indexing lets you select specific values, and how logical values can be used to filter a vector.
The point of this chapter is control: selecting the values you mean to select, checking whether your selection worked, and documenting your process clearly enough that someone else could follow it.
By the end of Chapter 4, you should be able to practice transparency in your notebook memos, select vector elements by position and name, build logical vectors using comparison operators, and use logical indexing to filter values from a vector.

title: Chapter 4: Structures
text:
R Notebooks—Part 2
In Chapter 3, you learned how to use an R Notebook (.Rmd) as a “reproducible thinking” document: code + output + memo-style writing in one place, in order. This section is a quick setup review before you begin the Chapter 4 work.
Here’s what you can do now:

Create and save an R Notebook (File > New File > R Notebook) and store it in your course folder.
Recognize the YAML header at the top of the file and edit the title.
Insert code chunks using the Insert button, a shortcut, or typed fences, and use chunks to organize the R code in your notebook.
Run chunks using the play button, Run menu, or keyboard shortcuts and view output below the chunk or in another relevant pane, depending on your RStudio settings.
Memo correctly:

Inside a code chunk: explanatory text must start with #; otherwise, R tries to run it as code.
Outside a code chunk: write normal paragraphs with no # needed.
Use the notebook to document your learning process, including your goal, checks, explanations, and resources used.


An R Notebook is only useful if a person can read and understand it. In this chapter, you will keep building clean notebook habits: preserving the YAML header, organizing your work clearly, writing readable memos, and preparing a notebook that can knit successfully to HTML.

Default Text
🎯 Please open a new R Notebook in your course folder named chapter4_notes.Rmd.
When you create a new R Notebook or R Markdown file, RStudio provides a template. It is designed to demonstrate the three core components of a notebook:

The YAML header: The block of text at the very top, enclosed between two lines of three dashes (---). This tells RStudio how to knit, or render, your document.
Markdown text: Text outside code chunks, such as “This is an R Markdown Notebook.” This shows you how to write regular prose.
Code Chunks: Fenced blocks containing code, such as plot(cars). This shows you how to embed executable R code.


Clear the Default Notebook Body
To start fresh, delete all the default text in the R Notebook so you have a blank canvas to work with.

Keep the Header
Do not delete the text at the very top between the --- lines. This is the notebook’s metadata, including its title and output format. If this header is deleted or malformed, the notebook may not render as intended.
Your header should look something like this:
---
title: "Chapter 4"
output: html_notebook
---
Keep this top section. Delete the example text and code below it.


Delete the Body
You can safely delete everything below the second --- line. Keep the YAML header at the top.

Place your cursor on the line immediately following the second ---.
Highlight everything all the way to the bottom of the document.
Press Delete or Backspace.



Save the Blank Notebook
After clearing the default text, save your blank notebook as chapter4_notes.Rmd in your course folder. This will be your working file for Chapter 4.


Type a memo
🗣 Add Comments: In 1–3 sentences, explain what you did to clear the default text and why you kept the YAML header.
I cleared the default text because the default text is just an example and I want to start with a blank notebook to practice writing my own memos and code. I kept the YAML header because it contains important information about the document, such as the title and output format, that control how the notebook is knitted.

🧐 Notice: Regular paragraph text outside a code chunk does not need #. Explanatory comments inside a code chunk do need # so R does not interpret them as code.

title: Chapter 4: Structures
text:
Applying Transparency
The Transparency module introduction explains why methods, decisions, checks, and resource use should remain visible. Chapter 3 introduced the R Notebook practices that support this record.
✍️ In this chapter, apply those practices to indexing and filtering. Add a short memo when you need to explain:

what value or group you intended to select,
whether you selected by position, name, or logical condition,
how you checked that the intended values were returned,
what an unexpected NA or omitted value showed,
and what resource helped if you used outside assistance.

You do not need every memo prompt for every line of code. Document choices and results that would be difficult to reconstruct later.

title: Chapter 4: Structures
text:
Indexing Vectors
The indexing operator [ is the standard way to extract parts of a vector. The basic pattern is x[i], where x is the vector and i is the index, or indices, of the elements you want to extract. For the atomic vectors in this chapter, [ ] can select one element or many, and it returns an object of the same type as x.
An index is a value used to identify elements in an object. In R, indices are often integers for positions, character values for names, or logical values such as TRUE and FALSE.

Positional Indexing
Positional indexing uses the numeric positions of elements in the vector to retrieve specific values.
🎯 Goal Use [ ] with index positions to extract values from a vector.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
z <- c(10, 20, 30, 40, 50) # create a vector


# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
z[1]       

[1] 10


🗣 This returns the first element by position.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
z[3]      

[1] 30


🗣 This returns the third element by position.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
z[2:4]     

[1] 20 30 40


🗣 This returns the second, third, and fourth elements by position.

🧐 Notice: z[2:4] selects positions 2 through 4. It does not search for the values 2, 3, and 4.


# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
z[-c(1, 5)] 

[1] 20 30 40


🗣 Negative indexing excludes specified positions from the returned result. z[-c(1, 5)] returns all elements except the first and last. The stored z object remains unchanged because the result was not assigned to an object.

🧐 Notice: R counts positions starting at 1, not 0. Negative positions exclude those positions from the returned result. They do not delete values from the original vector.



Character Indexing
When a vector has names, you can use those names to index into the vector. Character indexing uses the names of the elements to retrieve specific values.
There are two different naming ideas here.

Object name is the variable name nerdy_palette that you use to refer to the entire vector.
Element names are the labels assigned to each element within the vector (e.g., "Octarine", "TARDIS Blue").

Element names can be used in indexing to access specific elements of the vector. A named vector works like a small lookup table: each value has a label, and you can use the label to retrieve the matching value.
🎯 Goal: Create a named vector of color codes, then use character indexing to return the hexadecimal color code for "Octarine".

# Create nerdy_palette
nerdy_palette <- c(
  "Octarine" = "#7F00FF",
  "TARDIS Blue" = "#003B6F",
  "Rebeccapurple" = "#663399",
  "Hooloovoo" = "#4F97A3",
  "Cosmic Latte" = "#FFF8E7",
  "Vantablack" = "#000000",
  "Matrix Green" = "#03A062",
  "Source Engine Magenta" = "#FF00FF",
  "Command Red" = "#CC0000",
  "Impossible Green" = "#4D9E68"
)

# Use character indexing to return the hex code for Octarine
nerdy_palette["Octarine"]

 Octarine 
"#7F00FF" 


🗣 When you run this chunk, it should return the hexadecimal color code for "Octarine" from the nerdy_palette vector.
Character indexing requires exact matching on names. If you ask for a name that doesn’t exist, you get NA for that element.
🎯 Use character indexing to retrieve the color codes for “Octarine,” “TARDIS Blue,” and “NotAColor” from the nerdy_palette vector.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
nerdy_palette[c("Octarine", "TARDIS Blue", "NotAColor")]

   Octarine TARDIS Blue        <NA> 
  "#7F00FF"   "#003B6F"          NA 


🗣 The output should return the color codes for "Octarine" and "TARDIS Blue", plus NA for "NotAColor" because that name does not exist in the vector.


More Indexing by Position
🎯 Use positional indexing to return the first and third color codes from the nerdy_palette vector.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
nerdy_palette[c(1, 3)]

     Octarine Rebeccapurple 
    "#7F00FF"     "#663399" 


🗣 The output shows the hexadecimal color codes for Octarine and Rebeccapurple in the nerdy_palette vector.
We will return to indexing in later chapters when we learn about data frames.

title: Chapter 4: Structures
text:
Logical Vectors
📖 Review from Chapter 2.
Logical vectors are used for conditions and comparisons.
🎯 Create a logical vector named real that contains the values TRUE, FALSE, and NA using the c() function.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
real <- c(FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, NA)


# ✅ Check the real vector
print(real)

 [1] FALSE  TRUE  TRUE FALSE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE    NA


🗣 The output prints the logical values stored in the real vector.


Comparison Operators
Logical vectors can also be created using comparison operators. These operators compare values and usually return TRUE or FALSE. A comparison involving a missing value will usually return NA because R cannot determine whether the comparison is true or false.
Comparison operators include:

> greater than
< less than
== equal to
>= greater than or equal to
<= less than or equal to
!= not equal to

🎯 Create a logical vector named logicals that contains the results of the following comparisons: 1 > 2, 3 < 5, and 4 == 4 using the c() function.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
logicals <- c(1 > 2, 3 < 5, 4 == 4) 


# ✅ Check the logicals vector
print(logicals)

[1] FALSE  TRUE  TRUE


🗣 The output shows the results of the comparisons stored in the logicals vector. There is one FALSE value and two TRUE values. The first value is FALSE because 1 is not greater than 2. The second value is TRUE because 3 is less than 5. The final value is TRUE because 4 is equal to 4.


Logical Indexing
Logical indexing uses a logical vector inside [ ]. Values paired with TRUE are kept, and values paired with FALSE are left out. An NA in the logical vector produces an NA in the result because R cannot determine whether the matching value should be kept.
🎯 Create a new vector called smaller that contains only the values in number_list that are less than or equal to 20.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
number_list <- c(10, 25, 5, 30, 15, 40)

🗣 The number_list vector contains the values 10, 25, 5, 30, 15, and 40.

# ⚡ Step 1: create the logical "mask"
mask <- number_list <= 20

# ✅ Check the mask
print(mask)

[1]  TRUE FALSE  TRUE FALSE  TRUE FALSE


🗣 This prints a logical vector (TRUE/FALSE) the same length as number_list. Each TRUE marks a value that is less than or equal to 20.
⚠️ For predictable logical indexing, use a logical vector with the same length as the vector being filtered. If the logical vector is shorter, R may recycle it. If it is longer, the result can extend beyond the available values and include NA. A length mismatch is a reason to stop and check the mask.

# ⚡ Step 2: use the logical vector inside [ ]
smaller <- number_list[mask]
print(smaller)

[1] 10  5 15


🗣 This keeps only the values where mask is TRUE, so smaller contains 10, 5, and 15.
The key idea is that the condition number_list <= 20 creates a logical vector, and [ ] uses that logical vector as a filter.

title: Chapter 4: Structures
text:
Summary
In this chapter, you strengthened your R Notebook habits by practicing transparency in your code memos. You learned to document your goals, explain what your code produced, verify your results, and record outside resources when you used help. These habits make your work easier to understand, check, revise, and share.
You also learned how to select values from vectors. You practiced positional indexing to select elements by number, negative indexing to exclude positions from a returned result, and character indexing to select elements from named vectors. You saw that character indexing requires exact matching and returns NA when a requested name does not exist.
Finally, you learned how logical vectors support filtering. You created logical values with comparison operators, stored those results in a logical vector, and used logical indexing to keep only the values that met a condition.
Your main takeaway is that transparent notebooks make your coding choices inspectable, and indexing gives you control over which vector values you select or filter.

title: Chapter 4: Structures
text:
Chapter Terms
Character Indexing: Indexing a named vector using element names (character strings) instead of numbers. Names must match exactly; a missing name returns NA.
Code Chunks: Fenced blocks in an R Markdown or Quarto document that contain executable code, usually beginning with ```{r} and ending with three backticks. Code in a chunk can run interactively or during rendering. Depending on RStudio settings, output may appear below the chunk or in another relevant pane.
Comparison Operators: Operators that compare values. Common comparison operators are ==, !=, <, >, <=, and >=. They usually return TRUE or FALSE; a comparison involving a missing value will usually return NA.
Element Names: The individual labels assigned to elements inside a named vector (for example, "Octarine" or "TARDIS Blue"). Element names let you index by label (e.g., nerdy_palette["Octarine"]) to retrieve specific values.
Index: A value used inside a subsetting operator to identify which part of an object to extract or replace. In R, an index can use positions, names, or logical values; for example, x[2] uses a positional index to select the second element, while df[rows, columns] uses row and column indices to select parts of a data frame. R documentation also calls these values indices or subscripts.
Indexing Operator: The single square-bracket operator [ used to extract or replace selected parts of an object. For a vector, x[i] returns the elements identified by the positions, names, or logical values supplied in i.
Logical Indexing: Using a logical vector inside [ to select values. TRUE keeps the matching value, FALSE excludes it, and NA produces an unknown element represented by NA. A shorter logical index may be recycled, so checking that the index and source vector have the same length helps prevent unintended results.
Logical Mask: A logical vector used inside the single square-bracket operator [ to filter another object. TRUE keeps the matching value, FALSE excludes it, and NA produces an unknown element represented by NA. For predictable results, the mask should have the same length as the object being filtered.
Logical Vector: A vector that stores TRUE, FALSE, and sometimes NA for missing values. Logical vectors are commonly produced by comparisons, such as x > 0, and are used for filtering and conditional code.
Markdown: A lightweight plain-text formatting syntax used to write structured documents (headings, lists, links, emphasis, code) in a way that stays readable as plain text and can be rendered into formats like HTML on many platforms and tools.
NA: A special constant that marks a missing value (“Not Available”)—meaning the data point is unknown or not recorded. R also provides typed missing values like NA_integer_, NA_real_, NA_character_, and NA_complex_ to match the underlying data type.
Named Vectors: Vectors that have labels attached to their elements via the names() attribute, so you can refer to values by name instead of only by position. Named vectors are useful as simple lookup tables (for example, retrieving a hex code by a color name).
Negative Indexing: Using negative integers inside [ to exclude positions from the returned result. For example, x[-2] returns every element except the second. The original object remains unchanged unless the result is assigned to an object. Positive and negative indices cannot be mixed in the same subset, except for 0.
Object Name: The variable name you assign with <- that refers to the entire object in your environment. You use the object name to print, modify, or pass the whole object to functions.
Positional Indexing: Indexing a vector using numeric positions (for example, x[1] for the first element or x[c(1, 3)] for the first and third). Positions are based on the current order of the vector.
R Notebook: An .Rmd document that combines written explanation with executable R code chunks. Depending on your RStudio settings, interactive output may appear below a chunk or in another relevant pane. Rendering creates a finished document that keeps the writing, code, and computed output together.
YAML Header: The metadata section at the top of an R Markdown or Quarto document, written between --- lines, that controls document settings like the title, author, date, output format (HTML/PDF/Word), and options for rendering.

text:
📝 Practice Space

Before you begin:

Create a new R Notebook in RStudio.
Save it in your course folder as chapter4_practice.Rmd.

🪞 Reflect asks you to explain your thinking process, what confused you, what changed in your understanding, or what strategy you would use next.

These are there to help you practice the habit of writing memos as you work. Keep responses short: 1–3 thoughtful sentences is enough. For this Practice Space, answer the 🗣 Add Comments prompt for each coding task. Then answer 🪞 Reflect prompts where your thinking, prediction, confusion, or troubleshooting changed.
If you encounter an error, practice tenacity by choosing an informed next step. Practice ✍️ transparency by recording what happened, what you tried, what you checked, and what remains unclear. If a resource helped you troubleshoot, identify it and explain what it contributed.
If you use generative AI, follow the policies or guidance that apply to your work. Document the tool, what you asked, what the response contributed, and how you checked it. If you quote AI output, mark it clearly as quoted material and explain in your own words why you included it.
Before you finish, clear your Environment and run the notebook from top to bottom. Then knit to HTML to check that the notebook works in order.

Task 1
🧑‍🎓 Create a named vector
Practice creating a named vector by pairing values with element names. Some labels and some values are missing. The blanks test both parts of the name-value pair.
💡 Tip: Remember to include quotes around the element names.
🎯 Create a named vector called student_counts that stores the number of students in four campus groups. Use the exact group names and counts: "First Year" count is 18, "Sophomore" count is 22, "Junior" count is 16, and "Senior" count is 14.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook. Fill in the blanks.

)

# ✅ Check the vector

🗣 Add Comments: In 1–3 sentences, explain what print(student_counts) shows. Include how the group names help you understand what each number means.

Task 2
➖ Use negative indexing
Practice using negative positions inside [ ] to return all elements except selected positions.
🎯 Use negative indexing by placing a negative sign before c() to return all quiz scores except the values in positions 1 and 5.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook.
quiz_scores <- c(85, 92, 78, 88, 61, 95)

# ⚡ Fill in the blank to exclude positions 1 and 5 from the output.
quiz_scores[____(1, 5)]

🗣 Add Comments: In 1–3 sentences, explain which quiz scores were excluded from the output and which scores remained. The original quiz_scores vector still contains all six scores unless a new result is assigned to it.
The output excluded __________.
🪞 Reflect: How did you know that 1 and 5 meant positions, not score values? Explain what you would check if the output removed the wrong scores.


Task 3
🏷️ Use character indexing
Practice selecting a named vector element using an exact character name.
🎯 Use character indexing to retrieve the number of "Junior" students from the student_counts vector you created in Task 1.

# ⚡ Fill in the blank with the exact element name.
____["____"]

🗣 Add Comments: In 1–3 sentences, explain what the code returns. Include both the name and the value shown in the output.
🪞 Reflect: Does the exact spelling of "Junior" matter here? Why? Explain what you would check if R returned NA or did not find the value.


Task 4
⚖️ Create a logical vector
Practice using a comparison operator to create a logical vector.
🎯 Create a logical vector called meets_goal that checks whether each value in the quiz_scores vector from Task 2 is greater than or equal to 80.

# ⚡ Use the quiz_scores vector from Task 2.

# ⚡ Fill in the blank with the correct comparison operator.
meets_goal <- quiz_scores ____ 80

# ✅ Check the logical vector
print(meets_goal)

🗣 Add Comments: In 1–3 sentences, explain what each TRUE and FALSE means in meets_goal. Be specific about the cutoff value of 80.
`TRUE` means __________. `FALSE` means __________.
🪞 Reflect: Before running the code, how many TRUE values did you expect? Explain how you compared your prediction to the printed output.


Task 5
🔎 Use logical indexing
Practice using a logical vector as a mask to filter another vector.
🎯 Use meets_goal from Task 4 to keep only the values in quiz_scores that are greater than or equal to 80.

# ⚡ Use the logical vector from Task 4 to filter quiz_scores.
passing_scores <- ____[____]

# ✅ Check the new vector
print(passing_scores)

🗣 Add Comments: In 1–3 sentences, explain which scores were kept in passing_scores and why those scores matched the meets_goal mask.
`passing_scores` kept __________ because __________.
🪞 Reflect: Explain how the logical vector worked like a filter. What would happen if meets_goal had FALSE in a position where you expected TRUE?


Task 6
🪞 Reflect on logical masks
🎯 In 1–3 sentences, explain how the logical mask controls which values are kept from quiz_scores. Use the words TRUE, FALSE, and position in your answer.


Task 7
✅ Final checks
🎯 Step 1: Save your notebook.
Save the current version of chapter4_practice.Rmd.
🎯 Step 2: Sweep your Environment. Start clean.
Click the 🧹 broom icon in the Environment pane to clear objects.
🎯 Step 3: Run everything from top to bottom.
Use Run → Run All to execute every chunk in order. If an error appears, document what happened, what you tried, and how you resolved it or what remains unclear.
🎯 Step 4: Knit to HTML.
Knit your notebook to HTML to check that the document works from beginning to end.
🎯 Step 5: Review your work.
Review the rendered HTML. If you make corrections to the .Rmd file, repeat the clean run and knit. Follow any submission directions provided by your instructor.

title: Courage
text:
Courage while learning R
Learning R can make uncertainty visible. An error message may show that you do not yet understand what happened. A failed knit may expose a problem you cannot immediately locate. Asking a question may require admitting that you are confused. These moments can create fear of struggling, failing, appearing unprepared, or discovering that your current approach does not work.
Courage is the learning skill of continuing to pursue understanding when fear, uncertainty, or a perceived risk might otherwise direct your choices. Courage does not require pretending that a risk is absent. It involves responding in a way that serves learning: examining the evidence, acknowledging what you do not know, asking an appropriate question, or trying an informed next step.
Baehr (2022) describes intellectual courage as keeping fear from controlling intellectual activity. King (2021) adds an important qualification: persistence under threat is not automatically virtuous. Courageous learning requires a worthwhile goal, an appropriate occasion, sensible methods, and a motive directed toward knowledge. That said, persisting with an unproductive approach is not the kind of courage you should practice.
King describes virtuous courage as standing between two vice counterparts. Cowardice gives threats too much weight, or gives the value of learning too little weight, and can lead someone to withdraw from a worthwhile intellectual activity too soon. Rashness, on the other hand, gives threats too little weight and can lead someone to persist beyond what is wise. This distinction helps us evaluate whether an action fits the goal, occasion, means, and motive instead of treating every act of persistence as courageous.
Difficulty acting does not indicate a character failure. Anxiety or prior negative technology experiences can make intellectual risks more difficult. The purpose of this learning skill is not to label anyone as rash, courageous, or cowardly. It is to help you recognize manageable opportunities to act in support of your learning.
Courage in R may involve looking closely at an error, testing a possible explanation, consulting documentation, asking someone for help, or stating that a result does not yet make sense. It can also mean stopping an unproductive approach and seeking help from additional resources.
A growth mindset can support these actions. If you treat your current ability as something that can develop, an error or failed attempt can provide information about what to learn next. The goal is not to prove that you already know the answer. The goal is to remain engaged long enough to understand the problem and respond thoughtfully.
Courage works alongside the learning skills from earlier modules. Tenacity helps you continue through difficulty or frustration. Transparency helps you visualize your learning process with record of what you tried, misunderstood, and discovered. Courage helps you take the next appropriate intellectual step.

title: Courage
section: How courage appears in this book
text:
How courage appears in this book
The lion 🦁 marks courage. In this module, it appears when you are asked to take an informed step toward help, use an appropriate resource, or reconsider an approach that is not producing useful information.
The lion may mark opportunities to:

use an error message to decide what to inspect next,
consult an R help page, documentation, or a working example,
bring the relevant code, error message, and previous attempts when asking someone for help,
pause when repeated attempts are not productive,
and change your approach before persistence becomes rashness.

Naming what you do not understand and recording how you worked through it are Transparency practices. They remain important and may be modeled in these chapters. The lion marks the courageous action of seeking help, consulting a resource, or choosing a more productive strategy.

title: Courage
text:
What to focus on
As you work through Courage, practice four habits:

read error messages and other feedback for information about what to do next,
recognize when another attempt will test a new idea and when it will only repeat an unsuccessful approach,
seek help before confusion grows into hours of unproductive work,
and use what you learn from a resource or another person to return to the problem with a more informed strategy.

Courage means making a thoughtful decision about when to persist, when to change your approach, and when to ask for help. The goal is to keep learning without quitting prematurely or persisting beyond what is useful.

text:
Overview
Chapter 5 focuses on making your R Notebook organized, reproducible, and shareable.
You will learn how to use Markdown and YAML to structure your notebook, then knit it into an HTML report that someone else can read without opening RStudio. You will also practice using R help files to understand functions, arguments, and examples.
The main goal of this chapter is to build confidence with the normal problem-solving process in R. Instead of trying to memorize everything, you will learn how to use help resources and document what you learned in a shareable report.
In this chapter, you will practice how to:

title: Chapter 5 Help!
text:
#️⃣ Format your R Notebook using Markdown headings.
🧾 Add basic document information in the YAML header.
📤 Knit an R Notebook into a shareable HTML report.
⚠️ Recognize common reasons a notebook fails to knit.
🛠 Use error messages and help files to troubleshoot problems.
🔎 Open and read R help pages for functions.
🧮 Identify required arguments and default arguments.
✅ Use help pages to solve a problem with missing values.
🦁 Practice deciding when to keep troubleshooting, when to change strategies, and when to ask for help.

title: Chapter 5 Help!
text:
R Notebook -> HTML Report
In this chapter, you will learn how to turn your R Notebook into a shareable HTML report. The report records both your results and the process you used to reach them. 🦁 Courage in this chapter means staying engaged when an error or unfamiliar help page creates uncertainty, using the evidence to choose a reasonable next step, and asking for help before the struggle becomes unproductive. The chapter models this process, and the Practice Space asks you to use it and document what you tried and learned.
🎯 Please open a new R Notebook and save it as chapter5_notes.Rmd in the folder you use for this chapter. Use this document to take notes and practice the chapter content.

Open RStudio → File → New File → R Notebook.
Save it in the folder you use for this chapter as chapter5_notes.Rmd.
Keep the YAML header at the top of the notebook. Delete only the sample body text and example code below the second --- line.


🧐 Notice: The YAML header is the block between the two --- lines at the top. Keep that block because it controls the notebook’s title and output format.


In the YAML header, update the title to match this chapter. The next section explains how to add a date.


YAML Date Field
The YAML header is the metadata “label” for your notebook. It controls document settings like the title, date, and output format.
Good document labels help future-you and anyone who reviews or continues the work understand what the file is, when it was created, and what kind of output RStudio should build. This is a small documentation habit, but it matters when you are trying to keep your work organized.
A basic YAML header looks like this:
---
title: "R Notebook"
output: html_notebook
---
🎯 Add a date to your notebook by editing the YAML header to include a date: field.
Method A. Hard Code
Manually type the date you created the notebook. Include quotation marks around the date.
---
title: "Chapter 5 Notes"
date: "May 25, 2026"
output: html_notebook
---
Method B. Dynamic Date
Use R code to generate the current date automatically each time you knit the document. The inline R expression `r Sys.Date()` retrieves the current date from your computer’s operating system. This follows the syntax: backtick (`), then r, a space, Sys.Date(), and a closing backtick (`). The backtick is located above the Tab key on most keyboards.
---
title: "Chapter 5 Notes"
date: "`r Sys.Date()`"
output: html_notebook
---
Inline R works in YAML when written exactly as shown above. Notice the backticks around `r Sys.Date()` and the quotation marks around the complete expression: date: “`r Sys.Date()`”. You can learn more about inline R in the 📝 Notebook Advanced Activity, but for now, you can copy and paste the above YAML section to add a dynamic date to your YAML header. Each time you knit the document, the date will update to the current date.

You’ll learn how to knit soon, but first, you need a clear structure inside the document. That is where Markdown headings come in.


Heading levels
Headings create the outline of your notebook. The number of # symbols controls the heading level.
# Biggest heading

Text here will be in paragraph font.

## Main section heading

Text here will be in paragraph font.

### Subsection heading

Text here will be in paragraph font.
The chapter HTML pages in this book were created using RStudio. Notice how headings create a structured outline and how font sizes change with each heading level.
🎯 Add headings to your Chapter 5 Notes.
