[Add any memos or notes here to help you remember how to set up your notebook, such as how to add a date to the YAML header.]

## Markdown structure

[Add any memos or notes here to help you remember how to format and navigate your report in RStudio.]

## Knit to HTML

# Built-in Functions

## Help Files
🎯 Work to complete the sections under each heading as you go through the chapter content. You can also add more headings and subheadings as needed to organize your notes and code.


Outline Menu
The “outline pane” in RStudio uses your Markdown headings to create a clickable map of your document. This document outline or outline menu in the Source pane shows your headings/subheadings. They act as “Jump To” menus, helping you move between tasks without scrolling through the whole notebook.




Figure 1. Screenshot of R Markdown formatting



Figure 1 shows an RStudio R Notebook with a Markdown section heading (for example, ## Markdown structure) in the editor and the Outline menu on the right. Markdown headings create the structured outline. The orange arrow points to the Outline button used to show or hide it. 💡 Tip: Clicking a heading in the Outline menu jumps to that section in the report.
In this example, # Notebook set up creates a main section heading.


The most common beginner mistake with #
Put a space between the # symbols and the heading text to ensure the heading formatting works correctly.
For example, ##Task 1 will not format as a heading, but ## Task 1 will.
The # symbol means two different things depending on where you type it.

Outside a code chunk, # creates a Markdown heading.

🎯 Type ### Task 1 under ## Markdown structure to create a subsection heading.
## Markdown structure

Heading levels are controlled by the number of `#` symbols when they are used outside code chunks.

### Task 1

Inside a code chunk, # creates an R comment. R ignores the comment when it runs the code.

🎯 Type # This is a comment inside a code chunk. inside a code chunk to create a comment. 💡 Tip: Click the Insert Chunk button in the toolbar (green C with plus sign) and choose R from the drop-down list.
## Markdown structure

Heading levels are controlled by the number of `#` when used outside of code chunks.
Compare what you typed with the image of the knitted result.

### Task 1

🎯 Make a comment inside a code chunk

```fny
# ⚡ This is a comment inside a code chunk.
cursed_seq <- c(4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42)
```

🗣 The `#` symbol has two different meanings in R Notebooks.

🧐 Notice: To write notes about your code, type # inside the code chunk. Write result memos and learning reflections outside the code chunk without #.


Now that you have the basics of Markdown structure, you will test whether the whole notebook is ready to become an HTML report.

title: Chapter 5 Help!
text:
Knit to HTML
When you 🧶Knit to HTML, RStudio creates a static report file that includes your formatted headings and text, your code, and the output produced when the code runs. RStudio saves the HTML file on your computer and opens it in a web browser. Opening the file in a browser does not publish it on the internet. The browser address points to a file on your computer, so another person cannot use that address to open your report. To share the report, send or upload the .html file itself.
Knitting is not the same as “running a chunk.” Running a chunk uses your current R session. This means that running a code chunk can succeed even if you wrote code out of order or if objects used already exist in your Environment.
Knitting is a stronger test. It runs the entire notebook from top to bottom in a fresh session, then builds an HTML report.

How to Knit
RStudio interfaces vary. You may have a 🧶Knit button, or you may see a Preview drop-down menu.
Option 1: Knit button
In the Source pane, click the Knit button (it looks like a ball of yarn with a knitting needle 🧶).




Figure 2. Screenshot of knit button



Figure 2 is a screenshot of RStudio showing the 🧶Knit button on the toolbar (highlighted by an orange arrow), which students can click to knit the R Notebook into an HTML document.
Option 2: Preview menu
In the Source pane, click the Preview drop-down menu and select Knit to HTML.




Figure 3. Screenshot of Preview button



Figure 3 is a screenshot of RStudio with the Preview menu opened; orange arrows highlight the Preview dropdown button and the Knit to HTML option, showing how to knit an R Notebook into a shareable HTML document (not just run a single code chunk).
Below is the result you get after knitting to HTML.




Figure 4. Screenshot of resulting HTML report



Figure 4 is a screenshot of the knitted HTML output in a web browser showing the notebook title (“Chapter5 Notes”), the subsection heading (“Task 1”), memos as regular paragraph text, and an R code chunk, demonstrating what you get after you Knit to HTML.
When you knit, RStudio automatically does three things:

Starts a fresh R session (your Environment does not count).
Runs your notebook from top to bottom in order.
Produces an HTML file you can view and share.

This is why knitting is the real test of “does this notebook work?” If it knits, someone else (including future-you) can see the workflow and results without needing to open RStudio.
✅ Check: Your notebook must create every object it uses in the notebook itself. Your Environment does not count. Knitting may reveal a code error you did not notice. That is useful information about the first place in your workflow that needs attention.



Sharing the HTML File
The HTML file is automatically saved in the same folder as your R Notebook, with the same name but an .html extension instead of .Rmd. If you have not yet saved your R Notebook, RStudio will prompt you to do so before knitting.
Example:

chapter5_notes.Rmd
chapter5_notes.html

or

chapter5_notes.nb.html


🧐 Notice: The HTML opens in your browser, but it remains a file saved on your computer. The address bar shows a local file path, not a public web address. Another person cannot open that local address.

When you open an HTML file, your browser displays a formatted version of your notebook, including code, output, and memos.
To share the report, 📤 send or upload the .html file itself. Do not copy and share the local address from your browser.
💡 Tip: Check the HTML first to make sure it is correct and shows the correct formatting.


Knit Errors
When you knit, the Render tab shows progress messages as R runs your notebook from top to bottom.
A successful knit has three visible signs:

The Render tab shows the process finishing without an error message.
Your notebook opens as a formatted web page in a browser window or in RStudio’s Viewer.
An .html file appears in the same folder as your .Rmd file.

🦁 Courage: A failed knit can feel frustrating or uncertain. Courage does not require you to ignore that feeling. Read the error, use it as evidence, and take one informed next step.

Read the error message in the Render tab.
Find the line or chunk that caused it. The error usually names a chunk or shows a line number.
Fix the first error you see. Many later errors are just “domino effects.”
Knit again.

✅ Check: A knit error is a “not yet” signal. What specific problem is R naming, and what evidence can guide your next step?
Common reasons knitting fails:

You wrote the code out of order, so an object exists in your Environment but is not created earlier in the notebook.
You forgot to include setup code, such as loading packages, creating objects, or reading files through the appropriate relative paths.
A chunk contains an error you did not notice because you never ran that chunk.







ImportantIf Pandoc says the .knit.md file does not exist



RStudio uses a converter called Pandoc after R runs the notebook. If the Render tab first says output file: filename.knit.md and then says that the same .knit.md file does not exist, try this simple reset first:

Save your .Rmd file and close RStudio.
Check that the .Rmd file is still in your Chapter folder. If you also see a file ending in .nb.html, delete only that file. Windows may show it as chapter5_notes.nb and label it Chrome HTML Document.
Reopen the .Rmd file and knit again. RStudio can create a new .nb.html file if it needs one.

Do not delete the .Rmd file. That is the file containing your work.
If the error continues:

Save a copy of the .Rmd file in a short, local folder path that is not inside OneDrive, another cloud-synced folder, a network drive, or a downloaded ZIP file. On Windows, an example is C:/Users/YourName/DATA-R155/Chapter5/.
Close RStudio, reopen the copied file from that folder, and knit again.
If it still fails, create the small setup_check.Rmd document from the Check Your Installation section in the same local folder and knit it.
If the setup check also fails, stop and ask for help. Send the complete Render tab text and run the following lines in the Console so you can include the results:


R.version.string
R.version$arch
RStudio.Version()$version
rmarkdown::pandoc_version()
rmarkdown::find_pandoc()

If Settings > System > About > System type says ARM-based processor, include that fact. The instructor may need to check whether your computer should use the Windows emulation setup for RStudio or the native ARM64 version of Positron. Do not install a separate copy of Pandoc or Quarto, change Windows emulation settings, or disable security software as a first step.


🦁 Courage: Know when to ask for help. If you have made two focused attempts or spent about 10 minutes without learning anything new, stop repeating the same strategy. Save the exact error message and the smallest relevant code chunk. Note what you tried, then ask a peer, instructor, tutor, or another appropriate resource for help.
Next, you will shift from building the report to writing code inside it.
💡 Tip: Knit after any meaningful formatting or code change. It is easier to find an error when it was caused by your most recent edit.

title: Chapter 5 Help!
text:
Built-in Functions
Now that your notebook can become an HTML report, you need code worth documenting inside it.
Many built-in summary functions take a whole vector as input and return one summary value, or a small set of values. These are summary functions because they reduce many values down to a smaller result.
In this section, you will practice calling a function and noticing the difference between the stored function object and the function call that actually runs.

Function Objects vs. Function Calls
A function object is an R object that performs a task when it is called. For example, mean is the function object used to calculate the average of a numeric vector.
🎯 Run mean in a code chunk to see the stored function object. Add the code chunk under # Built-in Functions.

# ⚡ Type mean in your R Notebook inside a code chunk
mean

function (x, ...) 
UseMethod("mean")
<bytecode: 0xa3c435cb0>
<environment: namespace:base>


🗣 R displays the definition of the mean function object.
🦁 You do not need to understand every detail yet. For now, notice that typing mean without parentheses displays the function instead of calculating a mean.
To make the function do its job, you have to call it. A function call runs the stored code. To call a function, you type the function name followed by parentheses (). Inside the parentheses, you must provide any required arguments. For example, to calculate the mean of a numeric vector, you call the mean() function and provide the vector as an argument. The vector is a required argument because the function needs it to perform the calculation.
📜 The SYNTAX (basic):
mean(x)
where x is the numeric vector you want to summarize.
🎯 Calculate the mean of the cursed sequence.

# 📖 Review
cursed_seq <- c(4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42)  

mean(cursed_seq)                     

[1] 18


🗣 The mean() function calculates the average of the numbers in the cursed_seq vector by summing them up and dividing by the count of numbers.

title: Chapter 5 Help!
text:
Help Files
Nobody memorizes every function or every argument. Looking in help is one way you stay engaged when you do not already know what to do or you have a question. Skilled R users look things up.
Typing a question mark before a function name opens its help file. For example, ?mean opens the help file for the mean() function. The Files pane usually contains several tabs, including the Help tab, which displays documentation for R functions.
🎯 Use ?mean to open the help file for the mean() function. Add the code chunk under ## Help Files.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
?mean

🦁 Test knit: If knitting fails, follow the Knit Errors steps and stopping rule.
🚀 Explore and Play: As we move through the remainder of the chapter, add meaningful headings and subheadings to your notebook to organize your notes and code as you wish.

No Required Arguments
Some functions do not have a required argument. For example, the Sys.Date() function returns the current date without needing any input.
🎯 Call the Sys.Date() function to get the current date from your computer’s operating system.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
Sys.Date()

[1] "2026-10-03"


🗣 The Sys.Date() function retrieves the current date from the system clock and returns it as a Date object.
🎯 Open the help file for the Sys.Date() function.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
?Sys.Date

🗣 The Sys.Date help page opens in RStudio’s Help tab. Note that Sys.Date() has no required arguments.
Scroll through the help file to find information about the function’s usage, arguments, and examples.

Usage: shows the function signature and defaults.
Arguments: what each argument does.
Examples: copy/run examples to learn patterns.


Sys.Date() is a friendly first example because it does not require an input. Most functions you use for data analysis will need at least one argument. Next, you will compare this to mean(), which needs a vector to summarize.


Required Arguments
Required arguments are the inputs a function needs to do its job.
🎯 Open the help file for the mean() function. Scroll through the help file to find information about the function’s usage, arguments, and examples.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
?mean   
help(mean)

🗣 The mean help page opens in RStudio’s Help tab. mean.default(x, trim = 0, na.rm = FALSE, ...) shows that x is a required argument, while trim and na.rm have default values.


Default Arguments
Default arguments are inputs with preset values that a function uses when you do not provide your own values. For example, the trim argument in the mean() function allows you to exclude a certain percentage of the lowest and highest values before calculating the mean.
The SYNTAX (with one default argument):
mean(x, trim = 0)
If you do not specify a value for trim, R uses the default value of 0, which means no values are excluded.
🎯 Calculate the trimmed mean of the cursed sequence, removing 20% of the lowest and highest values before computing the mean.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
mean(cursed_seq, trim = 0.2)  # drop 20% from each end first

[1] 15.5


🗣 The mean() function first removes 20% of the lowest and highest values from the cursed_seq vector, then calculates the mean of the remaining values. With 6 values and trim = 0.2, R trims 4 and 42, then averages 8, 15, 16, and 23.

✅ Check: How can you tell which arguments are required?
The main clue that x is required is that it has no = sign or default value next to it in the usage section. The other arguments have = signs, showing the default values that R will use if you don’t provide your own.
Some functions use ... (dot-dot-dot). That means “additional optional arguments may be allowed,” not required ones. For now, ignore ... until you are more advanced.
📜 Argument clue:

no = → usually required
= → R has a default value
... → extra optional arguments may be allowed; ignore this for now


🦁 You do not need to understand the whole help page before you can use one useful part of it.

title: Chapter 5 Help!
text:
Reading R Help Pages
Help pages are useful, but they are not written like beginner tutorials. They are written like reference pages. That means you need to learn where to look when you are trying to write, fix, or explain code. This section gives you a reading strategy for reading the help pages.

Open Help Page
If you know the function name, type a question mark before the function name.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
?mean

You can also use the help() function.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
help(mean)

🗣 The help page usually opens in the help tab in the bottom-right area of RStudio. That area contains several tabs, such as Files, Plots, Packages, Help, and Viewer.


Reading Order
When you open a help page, use this reading order:

Description: What does this function do?
Usage: What does the function call look like?
Arguments: What goes inside the parentheses?
Examples: What is one working pattern I can test?

For now, you may skim or skip sections like Details, Value, References, and See Also.


The Usage Section
The Usage section shows the basic recipe for writing the function call.
Open the help page for mean().

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
?mean

In the Usage section, you may see something like this:

## Default S3 method:
mean(x, trim = 0, na.rm = FALSE, ...)

Read the usage line like this:







Part
What it means




mean()
This is the function being called.


x
Required. This is the object you want R to average.


trim = 0
Optional. R uses 0 unless you choose a different value.


na.rm = FALSE
Optional. Missing values are not removed unless you choose TRUE.


...
Extra options may be allowed. Ignore this for now.




In summary:

a required argument is an input the function needs before it can do its job.
a default argument is an input R already has a value for. You can use the default value, or you can replace it with your own value.

🗣 In mean(x, trim = 0, na.rm = FALSE, ...), the argument x is required because it does not have a default value. The arguments trim and na.rm are optional because R already has default values for them.



Use the Help Page to Solve a Problem
Let’s use the help page for a troubleshooting task. We’ll create a vector with a missing value, try a calculation, notice an issue with the result, and then use the help page to decide which argument needs to change.
🎯 Create a vector with one missing value.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
messy_scores <- c(80, 90, NA, 100)

print(messy_scores)

[1]  80  90  NA 100


🗣 The third position is marked with NA, which means the numeric value is missing.
🎯 Try to calculate the mean of messy_scores using only default arguments.
💬 Prediction: What do you think R will return? Calculate your predicted answer before you run the code.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
mean(messy_scores)
class(messy_scores)

🗣 R returns NA because the vector contains a missing value. By default, mean() does not remove missing values before calculating the average. This means that R cannot calculate the mean of the vector due to the missing value.
🦁 We haven’t yet learned how to change that behavior. This is the moment to use the help page.
🎯 Open the help page for mean().

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
?mean

✅ Check: In the Arguments section, find the argument named na.rm.
🦁 Ask yourself:

What does na.rm control?
What default value does R use?
What value should I use if I want R to remove missing values?

🎯 Try the code again using na.rm = TRUE.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
mean(messy_scores, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 90


🗣 The argument na.rm = TRUE tells R to remove missing values before calculating the mean. This does not delete the missing value from your original vector. It only tells mean() how to handle the missing value during this calculation.

Next, you will see how help-page examples can give you working patterns even when they do not exactly match your task.


Examples
The Examples section is often one of the most useful parts of a help page. Examples show working patterns. Your job is to adapt the pattern to your own object.
You are using the example to understand a structure, then applying that structure to your own task.
🎯 Run R’s built-in examples for mean().

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
example(mean)

🗣 The example() function runs examples from the help page. You do not need to understand every line.
🦁 Help-page examples may look unfamiliar. Look for one pattern that helps you understand how the trim argument is used in the mean() function.


Unknown Function Name
So far, we knew the function name: mean().
Sometimes you know the topic, but you do not know the function name. For example, you might know you need help with missing values, but you may not know which function or argument to search for. In that case, use ?? or help.search().
🎯 Search for help pages related to “missing values” using ?? and help.search().

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
??"missing values"


# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
help.search("missing values")

🗣 Use a pattern such as ?mean when you already know the function name. Use ??"search words" or help.search("search words") when you know the topic but not the exact function.







Situation
What to type




I know the function name.
?mean


I know the function name and want another option.
help(mean)


I know the topic but not the function name.
??"missing values"


I want to search help pages for a phrase.
help.search("missing values")


I want to run built-in examples.
example(mean)

title: Chapter 5 Help!
text:
Document Help
Troubleshooting is part of working in R. Documenting your troubleshooting efforts makes that work visible. When you use a digital or human resource, document where you went, why, and what you discovered.
🎯 Add a short help note to your report.
Type the 👀 Cite, 🗣 Comment, and 🪞 Reflect statements as regular Markdown text. Put only runnable R code and R comments inside the code chunk.

👀 I used `?mean` to read about the `na.rm` argument.

🗣 The help page showed that `na.rm` defaults to `FALSE`. 
I changed `na.rm` to `TRUE` because my vector contained an `NA` value.

# ⚡ Code
messy_scores <- c(80, 90, NA, 100)
# ✅ Check
mean(messy_scores, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 90


🗣 The result is `90` because R averaged `80`, `90`, and `100` after removing `NA` from the calculation.

🪞 I learned that a default argument can be optional but still important. 
In this case, `na.rm` had a default value, but I needed to change it for my data.

🦁 If knitting fails, follow the Knit Errors steps and stopping rule.

🦁 Documenting your process of thinking helps you identify your understanding. It will increase self-awareness and help you regulate your cognitive processes. It will also help you prepare to ask for help when you need it. You will be able to show what you tried, what you learned, and what you need help with.

title: Chapter 5 Help!
text:
Summary
In this chapter, you strengthened your R Notebook habits by learning how to create a complete, shareable HTML report. You practiced editing the YAML header, using Markdown headings to organize your notebook, knitting your work to HTML, and sharing the actual .html file rather than a local browser address.
You also learned that knitting is the real test of whether your notebook works. Running a single chunk only checks part of the code in your current R session, but knitting runs the whole notebook from top to bottom in a fresh session. When knitting fails, the error message is feedback that helps you find what needs to be fixed next.
Finally, you learned how to use built-in R functions and help files. You practiced the difference between a function object and a function call, identified required and default arguments, used ?mean, help(), example(), and help.search() to find information, and changed na.rm = TRUE to handle missing values in a calculation.
Your main takeaway is that strong R work depends on organized notebooks, successful knitting, and the courage to use errors and help files as part of the coding process.

title: Chapter 5 Help!
text:
Chapter Terms
Arguments: Inputs that you provide to functions to customize their behavior. Arguments are specified within the parentheses of a function call and can modify how the function operates or what data it processes.
Default Arguments: Inputs that already have a preset value in the function definition and are used automatically when you don’t provide your own (e.g., mean(x, na.rm = FALSE) by default).
Examples Section: The part of an R help page that shows runnable code examples for how a function is used in practice. This section is often the fastest place to learn because it shows the function in context: what inputs go inside the function call, what the code looks like, and what kind of output to expect. In R, many help-page examples can also be run with the example() function.
Function Call: The act of running a function by writing its name followed by parentheses, optionally supplying arguments inside (e.g., mean(x)).
Function Object: A function stored as an R object (functions are “first-class” in R, meaning you can assign them to names, pass them to other functions, and inspect them).
Help Page: Documentation for R functions and packages that provides information on usage, arguments, and examples. For example, use ?mean or help(mean) to open the help page for mean().
Help Tab: Located in the Files/Plots/Packages/Help pane, this tab provides access to R documentation, package vignettes, and search functionality to find help topics related to R functions and packages.
HTML: A web page file type (.html) written in HyperText Markup Language that a web browser can open and display as a formatted document. Preview, Knit, or Render can create an HTML file (often .html or .nb.html) that shows your notebook’s text, code, and output. When the file opens from your computer, the browser address is a local file path, not a public link. Share the .html file itself.
Inline Code: Code-style text placed within a sentence by surrounding the text with single backticks, such as penguins. In Quarto and Markdown, inline code is used to mark object names, function names, file names, or short code expressions so they appear in a monospace code font in the rendered report. This formatting signals to the reader, “treat this as code or a code-related name,” not as ordinary prose.
Inline R: A short R expression written inside backticks with the prefix r (for example, `r Sys.Date()`) that is evaluated when you knit/render the document and replaced with its result in the output. Inline R is used to insert dynamic values (dates, computed statistics, labels) directly into your narrative text, and it can also be used in YAML fields like date: “`r Sys.Date()`” when supported.
Knit: In RStudio, the action that renders an .Rmd (including an R Notebook) into a finished output file (such as HTML, PDF, or Word) by running the document’s code chunks, inserting their results, and converting the document to the chosen format. Clicking the Knit button typically calls rmarkdown::render() in a new, clean R session, so everything needed to reproduce the result must be created or loaded in the document itself, and the output file is saved alongside the .Rmd.
Knit Button: The toolbar button in RStudio that renders an R Markdown file (.Rmd) into a finished output (e.g., HTML, PDF, Word) by calling rmarkdown::render() and running the document’s code to generate results. The output file is saved next to the .Rmd (same base name), and the button’s drop-down lets you choose among available output formats (shortcut: Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + K).
Outline Menu: A navigation tool in RStudio that uses your Markdown headings to create a clickable map of an .Rmd or .qmd document. The outline shows the structure of the notebook by heading level, so you can jump between sections without scrolling through the whole file. In RStudio, open it from the Outline button/menu in the Source pane toolbar.
Render Tab: A temporary tab that appears in RStudio’s Console pane when you Knit or Render an R Markdown (.Rmd) or Quarto (.qmd) document. It shows progress messages, warnings, and errors separately from your interactive Console, and typically includes a Stop control so you can interrupt a failed or long render.
Required Arguments: Inputs a function needs because they have no default value in the function definition; you must supply them in the call (or the function can’t do its job).
Usage Section: The part of an R help page that shows how to write the function call, including its arguments and any default values.
YAML Header: The metadata section at the top of an R Markdown or Quarto document, written between --- lines, that controls document settings like the title, author, date, output format (HTML/PDF/Word), and options for rendering.

title: Chapter 5 Help!
text:
📝 Practice Space
This Practice Space has two parts.
First, you will answer short multiple-choice questions that check whether you can organize an R Notebook, read an R help page, use a function argument, and explain why knitting is an important reproducibility check.
Second, you will practice troubleshooting an R Markdown file. Use the error messages and the troubleshooting workflow from this chapter to decide what to check and change.

Part 1: Check your understanding
Choose the best answer for each question in this section.

Task 1
🧾 YAML header
Which YAML header is the best match for a Practice Space Notebook that should knit to an HTML notebook?



---
title: "Chapter 5 Notes"
date: "`r Sys.Date()`"
output: html_notebook



--
title = "Chapter 5 Practice"
date = Sys.Date()
output = html_notebook
--



---
title: "Chapter 5 Notes"
date: "`r Sys.Date()`"
output: html_notebook
---



---
"Chapter 5 Notes"
"`r Sys.Date()`"
html_notebook
---



Task 2
#️⃣ Markdown headings
Which line correctly creates a level 2 Markdown heading called Help Pages?
A. ##Help Pages
B. ## Help Pages
C. # # Help Pages
D. Help Pages ##



Task 3
💬 Markdown heading vs. R comment
Which statement correctly explains the difference between # outside a code chunk and # inside a code chunk?
A. Outside a code chunk, # creates an R comment. Inside a code chunk, # creates a Markdown heading.
B. Outside a code chunk, # creates a Markdown heading. Inside a code chunk, # creates an R comment.
C. # always creates a Markdown heading no matter where it appears.
D. # always causes an error in R Notebooks.



Task 4
🧩 Required arguments and default arguments
The mean() help page may show a usage line like this:
mean(x, trim = 0, na.rm = FALSE, ...)
Which answer correctly identifies the required argument and one default argument?
A. x is required; na.rm = FALSE is a default argument.
B. trim = 0 is required; x is a default argument.
C. ... is required; x should be ignored.
D. na.rm = FALSE is required; trim = 0 is not an argument.



Task 5
🧮 Use a help-page argument to handle missing values
You create this vector:
daily_steps <- c(5000, 7500, NA, 10000)
Then you run:
sum(daily_steps)
R returns NA.
Which call to sum() correctly uses an argument to handle the missing value before adding the numbers?
A. sum(daily_steps, na.rm = TRUE)
B. sum(daily_steps, remove.NA = TRUE)
C. sum(daily_steps, missing = FALSE)
D. sum(daily_steps, delete = NA)



Task 6
📤 Reproducibility check
Which is a stronger reproducibility check: knitting an R Notebook to HTML or running every code chunk?
A. Running each code chunk is stronger because it checks only the selected code without rerunning earlier chunks.
B. Knitting is stronger because it checks Markdown formatting and creates an HTML file, but it does not rerun the code.
C. Knitting is stronger because it reruns the notebook from top to bottom in a clean session, so needed objects must be created in the document in the correct order.
D. Running each code chunk is stronger because it uses the objects already saved in the Environment, so the final report shows the most recent results.

title: Chapter 6: Missing Values
text:
Missing Values Workflow
The na.rm argument in the mean() function has a default value of FALSE. This means that mean() does not remove missing values before calculating. If the input contains NA, the result is usually NA.

Special Values
In R, missing values are represented by the special value symbol NA.
R has several special values that represent non-standard data states.

NA (“Not Available”) signals missing information: the value is unknown or unavailable. A value may be missing because it was not recorded, could not be measured, or does not apply.
NaN (“Not a Number”) signals an undefined numeric result, such as 0 divided by 0.


# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
0 / 0      # Produces NaN – undefined arithmetic

NA         # Built-in constant representing a missing value

🗣 R prints NA and NaN in the Console so you can spot them quickly. Even though they look similar, they do not mean exactly the same thing.

NA means the value is absent or unknown.
NaN means the result is not a valid number, usually because the math operation is undefined.

We will mostly focus on NA in this chapter because missing values are common in real datasets. Missing values can occur in datasets because of incomplete data entries such as non-responses in surveys, or when joining two datasets. R will do the operation, but the result becomes NA because the value is unknown; this is called propagation.
📜 The SYNTAX (with na.rm default argument):
mean(x, na.rm = FALSE)
where na.rm is a logical argument that tells the function whether to remove NA values before calculating the mean.
🎯 Add NA value(s) to the cursed sequence and calculate the mean while handling missing values.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
cursed_seq <- c(4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42, NA)  # includes a missing value
# cursed_seq <- c(cursed_seq, NA, NA)    # uncomment to add more missing values

mean(cursed_seq)                       # default is na.rm = FALSE → returns NA

mean(cursed_seq, na.rm = TRUE)         # Change default to TRUE to ignore missing values

🗣 The first mean() call returns NA because the default behavior leaves the missing value in the input, so the mean cannot be determined. The second call uses na.rm = TRUE to ignore the NA values, allowing the function to compute the mean of the remaining numbers.

In many summary functions, any NA in the vector causes the result to be NA unless you tell R to remove missing values first.








Function
What it does
Example




sum(), prod()
Sum/product
sum(x, na.rm = TRUE)


mean(), median()
Central tendency
mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)


min(), max(), range()
Extrema/range
range(x, na.rm = TRUE)


sd(), var()
Spread
sd(x, na.rm = TRUE)






Detecting Missing Values
A quick yes/no check prevents surprises later in your workflow.

anyNA(x) returns TRUE if any element in x is NA or NaN.

📜 The SYNTAX (basic):
anyNA(x)
where x is the vector you want to check for missing values.
🎯 Use anyNA() to check if there are any missing values in a vector.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
Vector_NA <- c(3, 7, NA, 12)  # Our sample data – one value is missing

anyNA(Vector_NA)              # TRUE means "Something is missing!"

🗣 If this were my data and I saw FALSE, I could relax; the vector has no gaps. Seeing TRUE tells me to investigate further.
🦁 If the result surprises you, pause before changing the code. Write what you expected, what R returned, and what you will check next.


Locating Missing Values
There are two useful functions to find the exact positions of missing values in a vector:

is.na(x) returns a logical vector: TRUE wherever x is NA or NaN.
which(logical_vec) converts TRUE positions into numeric indices, which are handy for slicing or replacing values using positional indexing.

🎯 Use is.na() and which() to locate missing values in Vector_NA.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
is.na(Vector_NA)          # Notice that it is TRUE at position 3

🗣 The is.na() function creates a logical vector indicating which elements are missing. The third element is TRUE, indicating that the third element in Vector_NA is NA.
Vectors can be quite long, so it’s often more useful to get the numeric indices of missing values. Use which() to extract those indices.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
logical_NA <- is.na(Vector_NA)
which(logical_NA)   # Returns index 3 directly

🗣 The is.na() function creates a logical vector logical_NA indicating which elements are missing, while the which() function extracts the indices of those missing values (see Positional Indexing).


Which Missing-Value Function Should I Use?
Several functions help you work with missing values. They answer different questions.








Question
Function
What it returns




Are there any missing values?
anyNA(x)
One TRUE or FALSE answer


Which values are missing?
is.na(x)
A logical vector


What positions are missing?
which(is.na(x))
Numeric index positions


How many values are missing?
sum(is.na(x))
A count


What proportion is missing?
mean(is.na(x))
A proportion



The key is to choose the function that matches your question. If you only need a quick yes/no check, use anyNA(). If you need the exact positions, use which(is.na(x)).

title: Chapter 6: Missing Values
text:
Nesting Function Calls
Nesting function calls means putting one function call inside another function call. The output of the inner function becomes an argument to the outer function. This works because functions return values. R can immediately pass a returned value into the next function.
You just used is.na() and which() in separate steps. You can also nest them.
🎯 Nest is.na() inside which() to find the missing position in Vector_NA.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
which(is.na(Vector_NA))

🗣 R runs is.na(Vector_NA) first, returning FALSE FALSE TRUE FALSE. Then which() returns the position of the TRUE value: 3. This is the same result you got when you stored the logical vector as logical_NA in the previous section.
🦁 If nested code is difficult to understand or debug, change strategies by separating it into smaller steps. Store and check each result before combining the functions again. The next section might be challenging to read, review 🦁 Change strategies: Check each step.
🎯 Use sample() to randomly select 5 numbers from the vector travel_jumps, then calculate the mean of those sampled numbers by nesting the sample() function inside the mean() function.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
travel_jumps <- seq(from = 1887, to = 2052, by = 33)
mean(sample(travel_jumps, size = 5, replace = TRUE))  # sample then average

R runs sample() first and passes its five selected values to mean(). You can also put the seq() call inside sample(), so all three steps appear in one expression:

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
mean(sample(seq(from = 1887, to = 2052, by = 33), size = 5, replace = TRUE))







Note🦁 Change strategies: Check each step



Now test each part of that expression. Start with the innermost seq() call, check its result, and then use that result in sample() and mean().

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
travel_jumps <- seq(from = 1887, to = 2052, by = 33)
travel_jumps                # ✅ Check: six numbers, from 1887 to 2052

sampled_jumps <- sample(travel_jumps, size = 5, replace = TRUE)
sampled_jumps                # ✅ Check: five sampled numbers

mean_jump <- mean(sampled_jumps)
mean_jump                    # ✅ Check: one mean

🗣 Separating the steps makes each intermediate result visible. If a result is unexpected, you can identify which step needs attention. Each call to sample() makes a new random draw, so the means from separate runs may differ even when the code follows the same steps.


Nesting can express several steps in one line, but the separated version is often easier to check. In later chapters, you will learn another way to write multi-step workflows using pipes.

Locating Missing Values with Nesting
🎯 Create a large vector with some missing values using sample() and c().

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
set.seed(100)
LargeVec <- sample(c(1:10, rep(NA, 10)))
print(LargeVec)

🗣 We used the c() function in Chapter 2. Here we have nested c() inside of sample(). We also used the rep() function, which is covered in more detail in a later chapter.
🎯 Use which() and is.na() to find the positions of missing values in a large vector by nesting the is.na() function inside the which() function.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
which(is.na(LargeVec))                    # ▶ Where are the gaps?

🗣 The is.na() function creates a logical vector indicating which elements are missing, and the which() function determines the indices of those TRUE values. The numbers are the numeric indices (positions) of the NA values.


Summarizing “Missingness”
As a researcher, knowing how much data is missing helps guide your next step, but the amount is only one part of the decision.
A single NA may matter if it occurs in a key measurement. A larger number of missing values may create a serious problem, depending on where the missing values occur and why they are missing.
For example, if 1 out of 20 values is missing, then 5% of the vector is missing. If 10 out of 20 values are missing, then 50% of the vector is missing. Those situations raise different concerns, but the percentage alone does not determine what you should do. Consider the amount and pattern of missing data, why the values may be missing, your analysis goal, the consequences of the decision, and guidance from your field.
🎯 Use sum() and mean() with is.na() to summarize missing values in a large vector.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
sum(is.na(LargeVec))    

mean(is.na(LargeVec))   

🗣 The sum(is.na(LargeVec)) expression counts the total number of missing values in LargeVec by summing the TRUE values from is.na(). The mean(is.na(LargeVec)) expression calculates the proportion of missing values by taking the mean of the logical vector returned by is.na(), where TRUE is treated as 1 and FALSE as 0. When 50% of the values are missing, the mean of the logical vector is 0.5.


Imputation
Now that you can detect and locate gaps, you have to decide what to do about them. There is no universal “best” choice because each option makes assumptions.
In this chapter, we’ll use mean imputation as a practice method for learning replacement logic. This is not a recommendation to use mean imputation in research. Replacing missing values with the mean can make the data look more complete than it really is, and it can distort the distribution, especially the variance.
🦁 If you do not know why values are missing, pause before removing or replacing them. Name what you do not know, check the data documentation, or ask someone who understands how the data were collected.

Option 1: Exclude missing values from a calculation or create a vector containing only observed values. This is simple, but it reduces the available data and can bias results if the missingness is systematic.
Option 2: Replace missing values with a summary value (simple imputation). This keeps the vector length the same, but it can distort the distribution, especially the variance.

In this chapter, we are practicing logical indexing on a single vector. In real analysis, values often live in rows of a dataset (one row = one person or observation) with multiple columns. If you remove rows because one column is missing, you also throw away valid information in other columns. That can:

shrink your sample size (less stable results),
change which groups are represented (bias),
change which observations contribute to plots, models, and group summaries.


🌳 Imagine a class dataset with student_id, major, exam1, and exam2. If exam2 is missing for some students, removing those students from the analysis (rows) means we’d also lose their exam1 scores and their major. If our goal is “average Exam 1 by major,” dropping rows because Exam 2 is missing can silently change the story. This is especially true if missing Exam 2 happens more in one major than another.

The bottom line is that there is no one-size-fits-all solution. The appropriate response depends on the amount and pattern of missing data, why values may be missing, your analysis goal, the consequences of the decision, and guidance from your field. For a summary of one variable, a summary function may omit NA values when doing so is defensible. In analyses with multiple variables, both removing and imputing values require justification. Keeping rows aligned or comparing groups does not, by itself, make imputation the right choice.
🦁 Whatever you choose, write a memo that documents the decision, the evidence you used, and what remains uncertain. Making your reasoning visible helps you evaluate the choice and ask a clearer question if you need help.
Next, you’ll practice both strategies on a vector so you can see the trade-off clearly. Later, you’ll apply the same decision logic to multi-column datasets.


Option 1
Remove missing values
🎯 Use indexing with !is.na() to keep only the observed (non-missing) values in LargeVec.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
clean_vec <- LargeVec[!is.na(LargeVec)]   # Keeps only observed values
clean_vec

🗣 is.na(LargeVec) returns a logical vector (TRUE for missing, FALSE for present). The ! flips it (so TRUE means “keep this value”). The brackets [...] then use that logical vector to select only the elements you want.






Note📖 Review: Check each part of the filter



Before using the full expression, run each part and inspect what it returns.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
print(LargeVec)              # See the original values
LargeVec[2]                  # Review: select one value by position
is.na(LargeVec)              # TRUE where a value is missing
!is.na(LargeVec)             # TRUE where a value is present
LargeVec[!is.na(LargeVec)]   # Keep only the present values

✅ Compare the last result with clean_vec. They should contain the same observed values.





Option 2
Impute missing values (replace NA with the mean)
Now that you can detect and locate gaps, you have to decide what to do about them; one option is to impute missing values by replacing them with a summary value. It means “fill in missing values.” A common simple imputation method is to replace missing values with the mean of the observed values.
🎯 Make a copy of LargeVec, then replace only the missing values with the mean of the observed values.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
imputed <- LargeVec     # Make a copy to preserve original

🗣 The reason we make a copy is that we want to keep the original vector with its missing values intact for comparison. This way, we can see the effect of imputation without losing the original data.
💡 Tip: Once we make a copy, we use that copy name everywhere in the imputation line. This new version of the vector is called imputed, and it is the version we will use next. imputed is the vector’s name. The name is descriptive of what the difference will be between it and the original LargeVec once we have replaced only the missing values with the mean of the observed values. It is good practice to name objects in meaningful ways.
We’re doing three actions on the same object (imputed):
🎯 (1) identify missing positions, (2) compute a replacement value, and (3) write the replacements back.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
imputed[is.na(imputed)] <- mean(imputed, na.rm = TRUE)
imputed

🗣 is.na(imputed) identifies exactly where the gaps are, and imputed[...] <- ... replaces only those positions. The na.rm = TRUE setting is needed here to calculate the replacement mean from the observed values. Without it, mean(imputed) would return NA because the input contains missing values.
The object we are editing is on the left side: imputed[is.na(imputed)].
The object we are using to find the missing positions is inside brackets: is.na(imputed).
The general replacement pattern is:
object[positions_to_replace] <- replacement_value

🧐 Notice: You might think, “The missing values came from LargeVec, so I should check LargeVec.” But the rule is to use the same object we’re editing, or we risk indexing the wrong thing later. The object we are summarizing to compute the replacement value is also imputed: mean(imputed, na.rm = TRUE)


🧐 Notice: You might think, “mean of observed values” means “mean of the original” and want to use LargeVec. But imputed currently equals LargeVec, so the mean is identical either way at that moment. As soon as you start changing imputed, mixing names can cause logic bugs. You might replace values in one object using positions or summaries computed from a different object.

In summary, wherever an element in imputed is missing, we replace that position with the mean of imputed while ignoring missing values so it can calculate the mean.
✅ Confirm your result by comparing sum(is.na(LargeVec)) with sum(is.na(imputed)).

# ✅ 
sum(is.na(LargeVec))      # Original vector – should print number 10
sum(is.na(imputed))       # Imputed vector – should print 0

🗣 The first sum(is.na(LargeVec)) call counts the number of missing values in the original vector, which should be 10. The second sum(is.na(imputed)) call counts the missing values in the imputed vector, which should be 0, confirming that all missing values have been replaced.

title: Chapter 6: Missing Values
text:
Summary
In this chapter, you strengthened your R workflow by learning how to recognize and handle special values in R. You practiced the difference between NA, which means information is missing, and NaN, which means a numeric result is undefined. You also learned that missing values can quietly affect your calculations because many R functions return NA unless you tell them how to handle missingness.
You built a practical missing-values workflow. You practiced using anyNA() to check whether missing values exist, is.na() to identify which values are missing, which() to locate their positions, sum(is.na(x)) to count missing values, and mean(is.na(x)) to calculate the proportion missing. You also practiced using na.rm = TRUE so summary functions can calculate results while ignoring missing values.
Finally, you practiced two basic strategies for handling missing values: removing missing values with logical indexing and replacing missing values with a simple imputed value. You also practiced nesting function calls so that one function’s result can be passed directly into another function. Your main takeaway is that strong R work depends on checking assumptions, understanding defaults, documenting your choices, and making sure your code is not only running, but producing results you can trust.

title: Chapter 6: Missing Values
text:
Chapter Terms
Impute: To replace missing or unusable values (e.g., NA) with substituted values, often using estimates based on the observed data (such as mean/median imputation or model-based predictions), so the dataset can be analyzed without dropping incomplete cases. Because imputed values are estimates, you should document what method you used and why.
Missing Values: Data values that are unknown or unavailable; in R they are represented by NA (“Not Available”). Depending on the context, a missing value may not have been recorded, may not have been measurable, or may not apply. NA is a special missing-value indicator (with typed versions like NA_integer_, NA_real_, and NA_character_), and many calculations will return NA if any missing values are present unless you explicitly remove them for that calculation (often via na.rm = TRUE, which defaults to FALSE in functions like mean()).
NA: A special constant that marks a missing value (“Not Available”), meaning the data point is unknown or unavailable. R also provides typed missing values like NA_integer_, NA_real_, NA_character_, and NA_complex_ to match the underlying data type.
NaN: A special numeric constant (“Not a Number”) that represents an undefined arithmetic result in floating-point math (for example, 0/0 or other invalid operations). NaN is non-finite (not a regular number).
Nesting Function Calls: Writing one function call inside another so the inner function runs first and its returned value becomes an argument to the outer function (for example, mean(sample(x, 5))). This works because a function call can appear anywhere an expression is allowed, and functions return a value that can be passed directly into the next call.
Positional Indexing: Indexing a vector using numeric positions (for example, x[1] for the first element or x[c(1, 3)] for the first and third). Positions are based on the current order of the vector.
Propagation: R’s default behavior where an unknown value “spreads” through a computation. If an expression includes NA, the result will usually be NA (e.g., 5 + NA returns NA) because the outcome can’t be determined without the missing information. This is often called NA propagation, and it’s why many summary functions return NA unless you explicitly remove missing values (e.g., na.rm = TRUE).
Special Values (NA, NaN, Inf, -Inf, NULL): Reserved constants in R that represent non-standard values: NA for missing data, NaN for undefined numeric results, Inf/-Inf for positive/negative infinity, and NULL for “no value” (an empty/null object). In practice, use is.na() to detect NA and NaN, is.nan() to detect NaN specifically (not NA), is.infinite()/is.finite() to handle infinities and other non-finite values, and is.null() to test for NULL.

Task 2
🛠 Build a random data set
🎯 Create scores as 28 values. That means you will create 25 random integers from 60 through 100, then add 3 missing values (NA) at the end.

First, use seq() to create the possible score values from 60 through 100. Store that sequence as pool.

💡 Tip: For this task, practice using seq() with separate inputs for the starting value and ending value. Do not use the : shortcut inside seq() here. If you are unsure what arguments seq() expects, look at ?seq and focus on the Usage line.

Then use sample() to draw 25 values from pool, with replacement. Store those sampled values as scores_numbers.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook, Fill in the blanks

🗣 Add Comments: Explain why scores has 28 elements even though sample() only drew 25 values.

Task 3
⚠️ Handle missing data
🎯 Using scores from Task 2:

Count missing values. Store as n_missing.
Compute the mean with defaults. Store as average_raw.
Compute the mean excluding NAs and store it as average_score.
Explain why average_raw behaves the way it does (use the word “default”).


n_missing <- ____                 # hint: is.na() + sum()


# ✅ Check the number of missing values
____        # should print 3


# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook, Fill in the blanks
average_raw <- mean(____)         # what happens?
# ✅ Check the result
____                              # should print NA


# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook, Fill in the blanks
average_score <- mean(____, ____)

title: Autonomy
text:
Autonomy while learning R
Learning R involves decisions. You decide how to organize your files, which information in an error message matters, what kind of object a function needs, which method fits your goal, and whether you should continue investigating or consult another resource. These decisions require more than following a sequence of instructions. They require you to understand what you are doing and take responsibility for what you do next.
Baehr (2022) describes intellectual autonomy as thinking for yourself and developing command of your own intellectual abilities. An autonomous learner can do more than repeat information or reproduce an example. The learner can explain an idea in their own words, apply it in a new situation, and use evidence to form a judgment.
King (2021) explains that autonomy requires appropriate reliance on others. Taking responsibility for your thinking does not require you to learn alone. A learner can rely too heavily on another person or source and allow that source to become a substitute for personal understanding. A learner can also reject useful instruction, evidence, or expertise in an attempt to remain independent. Autonomous learners use support without surrendering responsibility for their own conclusions.
Autonomy is the learning skill theme for this module. It means taking ownership of your understanding, choices, code, and learning. You can use instructions, examples, documentation, peers, instructors, and AI tools as resources. You remain responsible for deciding how that information applies, checking whether it is accurate, and understanding the work you produce.
Autonomy in R begins with knowing your goal and using evidence to decide what to do next. You might inspect your working directory, check whether R can see a file, read an error message, compare two objects, or examine the kind of output a function returned.
Autonomy also involves choosing among valid approaches. You may need to decide whether to use a graphical interface or code, whether to keep a column as a data frame or extract it as a vector, or whether to write a logical condition directly inside an index or save it as a separate object that you can inspect.
When a person, example, website, or AI tool suggests code, examine the suggestion before adopting it. Run the code, inspect the result, and decide whether it accomplishes your goal. You should be able to explain what the code does, why it fits the task, and what evidence shows that it worked.
Using help is part of autonomous learning. Courage may help you ask a question when you are uncertain. Autonomy helps you decide when support is appropriate, evaluate the guidance you receive, and use it to make an informed next decision.

title: Autonomy
section: How autonomy appears in this book
text:
How autonomy appears in this book
The compass 🧭 marks autonomy. It appears when you are being asked to orient yourself to the goal, examine the available evidence, and make a reasoned choice.
The compass may mark opportunities to:

decide whether you need detailed guidance or are ready to proceed,
organize files so you understand where your work and data are located,
inspect output or an error message before choosing the next step,
select an R method according to the kind of result you need,
test and evaluate code suggested by another resource,
protect original data while experimenting with a possible change,
and recognize when another resource or person can help you move forward.

The compass does not mean that you must solve every problem alone. It reminds you to use available support while remaining responsible for understanding and checking your work.

title: Chapter 7: Importing Data
text:
Overview
In earlier chapters, you learned how to write R code, use built-in functions, and work with missing values. In this chapter you do something more realistic: you bring datasets into R the way researchers do in actual projects.
Most import problems are not “R problems.” They are file management problems: the file is in the wrong folder, the file name doesn’t match, or the package you need wasn’t loaded. You will learn a simple, reliable workflow: download the data, put it in the same folder as your R Notebook, confirm R can see it, and then import it with the correct function.
Watch for the 🧭 autonomy marker throughout this chapter. It identifies places where you use evidence to make a choice, troubleshoot a problem, or decide when to seek help. Document these decisions in your Practice Space report.
This chapter is also structured differently. Many of the Practice Space tasks are built into the Guided Activity. If you complete each step as you go, you will finish the chapter with a working notebook that can knit successfully and reload your datasets from a clean start.
By the end of Chapter 7, you will be able to:

title: Chapter 7: Importing Data
text:
📊 Define tabular data and describe how rows and columns map to observations and variables in a data frame.
📂 Explain how the working directory affects file imports and compare the working directory used in the Console vs. during Knit.
🗂️ Organize downloaded data files in the correct folder and verify file visibility using list.files().
📦 Install required packages once and load required packages in an R Notebook so code runs from top to bottom when knitted.
💾 Load datasets from Base R and from installed packages using data() and confirm that the dataset is available in the Environment.
📥 Import CSV and Excel files using read_csv() and read_excel() and interpret the import feedback (rows/columns and column types at a basic level).
🆘 Troubleshoot common import failures (missing packages, wrong file location, wrong file name) using targeted checks (getwd(), list.files(), library()).

title: Chapter 7: Importing Data
text:
Data Management
One of the most common stumbling blocks to importing data is knowing where a file is stored on your computer.
A file path is the address to a file. When you write import code, R uses the file path to find the file you want to load. If R looks in the wrong folder, the import will fail even if your code is almost correct.
The first step to loading data into R is learning how to manage your files and folders so that R can find your data when you run code in the Console, run code in an Rmd file, or knit a Notebook, R Markdown, or Quarto document.

Folder Structure
Your course work should be stored in your main course folder:
Intro_to_R
For this chapter, create a new folder inside your Intro_to_R folder called:
Module_4
💡 Tip: Use Module_4 instead of Module 4 to keep the folder name easy to type consistently in file paths. R can work with spaces in folder and file names, but you must include each space exactly when you write the path.
Your folder structure should look like this:
Intro_to_R/
└── Module_4/

How to read folder structure diagrams
Here is how to read that folder structure:

Intro_to_R/ is your main course folder.
└── Module_4/ means Module_4 is inside the Intro_to_R folder.
The / at the end means the item is a folder, not a file.
The indentation matters. Anything indented farther to the right is nested inside the folder above it.

You may also see folder diagrams that use more symbols:

The / at the end means the item is a folder, not a file.

title: Chapter 7: Importing Data
text:
Working Directory
In Chapter 1, you learned how to use getwd() and setwd() to manage your working directory. This is crucial for importing data because R needs to know where to find the files you want to load.
Code that you run interactively uses the Console’s current working directory. When you Knit the notebook used in this chapter, R starts a fresh session and looks from the folder where the Rmd file is saved. Because these locations can be different, you will check both and compare the results.
🎯 Make R able to find your data files when you (1) run code in the Console and (2) when you Knit an R Notebook document.

Console
Check your working directory in the Console
🎯 Run in the Console.

# ⚡ Type this in the Console  
getwd()       
list.files()  






Example Console output after running getwd() and list.files().




✅ Look at the output from getwd() and list.files() in the Console. Notice which folder R is using and which files R can see there. The folder may be different from the one containing chapter7_practice.Rmd. You will compare it with the knitted notebook output next.
🗣 When you run getwd(), you are checking where R is currently “looking.” When you run list.files(), you are checking what R can actually see from that location.
🧭 If the file you need is not listed, your next move is to check whether the file is in the right folder or whether the working directory is set to the folder location where the desired file is saved.

The notebook works differently when you Knit it. For the notebook setup used in this chapter, R starts a fresh session and uses the folder where the Rmd file is saved. Let’s see that in action!


R Notebook
Check your working directory in the Notebook

Step 1
🎯 Add a new code chunk with the same code as above.

# ⚡ Type this in your notebook
getwd() 
list.files()

🧶 Test knit.

You should see the files for this chapter listed in the output:
[1] "car_prices.xlsx"              "chapter7_practice.Rmd"        "Values_Transport_dplace.csv"
🗣 When this notebook is knitted, R uses the folder where the Rmd file is saved as the working directory.
🪞 Reflect: Did R look in the same folder both times, or did the Console and Knit use different folders? Either result is okay. Explain what your result tells you about where R is looking. Why does this matter when importing files? This is Task 2 of the Practice Space at the end of this chapter.
