title: Chapter 7: Importing Data
text:
Import in R
This section shows you how to prepare R to import datasets. You will (1) install the packages needed for this chapter one time, and (2) load those packages every time you start a new R session so your notebook can run from top to bottom when you Knit.

📦 Packages refresher
To import data, we will need to use functions from additional packages that are not part of the base installation of R. A package is a collection of functions, data, and documentation that extends the capabilities of R. You were first introduced to packages in Chapter 3 when you installed rmarkdown to run your R Notebook.

Installing Packages
You need to download the package before you can use it. You only need to install the package once. Packages will need to be updated from time to time.
🎯 Install the packages you need for this chapter as a one-time action.
🧭 Choose either installation method below. Both install the same packages, so use the method that helps you understand and verify what R is doing.
Method A: GUI
Bottom-right pane → Packages tab → Install → type the package name.
In the bottom-right pane, you will see a tab called “Packages.” This is where RStudio lists the packages you have installed. You can install packages by clicking the Install button.



Click the 📥 Install button from the Packages tab then type dslabs in the Packages box and click Install to download dslabs from the Package Repository CRAN


🗣 After you click Install, notice the lines of code and message(s) that result in the Console. The code is what you would have to type if you were installing packages without using the GUI (Method B).
Method B: Type the code in the Console
Often, you will use the function install.packages() to install a package. This chapter uses readr to import CSV files, readxl to import Excel files, and dslabs to provide a curated dataset for practice.
🎯 Install the packages readr, readxl, and dslabs using install.packages().

# ⚡ Type this in your Console to install packages
install.packages("dslabs")                # You can install one package at a time
install.packages(c("readr", "readxl"))    # Or use c() to install multiple packages

🗣 The install.packages() function installs packages from CRAN. Messages during installation are normal. Warnings are also common and are often not fatal, but read them and use packageVersion() to confirm that the package installed. An error means the installation did not complete successfully. This code installs the dslabs, readr, and readxl packages. The c() function combines the package names into a vector, allowing you to install multiple packages at once.

⚠️ Common Pain Point: Run install.packages() in the Console rather than putting it in your R Notebook. If an installation line remains in the notebook, knitting may try to install the package again and may require internet access or additional input. Keep the library() lines in the notebook so the packages load when the notebook runs.


# ✅ Check
packageVersion("dslabs")

[1] '0.9.1'

packageVersion("readr")

[1] '2.2.0'

packageVersion("readxl")

[1] '1.5.0'


✅ Each packageVersion() line should print a version number. A version number means the package is installed on your computer. If you get an error saying there is no package with that name, the package did not install successfully.

After installing packages, you need to load them into your R session to use their functions. This is done with the library() function, which we will cover next.


Loading Packages
After installing the package, you need to load it into your R session using the library() function. This makes the functions in the package available for use. Every time you start a new R session, you will need to load the packages you want to use. To ensure your R Notebook works when you Knit it, you should include the library() calls in your R Notebook.
💡 Tip: Add headings and format your report as you work. 🎯 Add the heading # Library Packages.
🎯 Load the packages readr, readxl, and dslabs into your R session using a notebook code chunk so they load each time you Knit. This is Task 3 of the Practice Space at the end of this chapter.

# ⚡ Type this in a code chunk in the R Notebook to load packages
library(dslabs)  # For more datasets
library(readr)   # For reading CSV files
library(readxl)  # For reading Excel files

🗣 library() may print startup messages, and those messages are not automatically a problem. A normal startup message provides information about the package or session. An error means the package did not load.
🧶 Test knit.

Your folder system, notebook, and packages are now set up to import data. The next step is to learn how to load different sources of tabular data.

title: Chapter 7: Importing Data
text:
Tabular data
Tabular data is data that is arranged in a table format where rows represent observations and columns represent variables. Rows usually represent observations (cases, people, states, experiments, etc.). Columns usually represent variables (measurements you recorded). This is the most common format for datasets and what most people think of when they think about data. When you import data into R, it is often stored as a data frame.
A data frame (df) is the most common way to store tabular data in R. It is a two-dimensional table made of rows and columns. Data frames are rectangular. Every column must have the same number of rows. In other words, each column must be the same length, because every row must have a value (or an NA) for every column. A data frame can store different data types in different columns (numbers, characters, logical values, etc.). A practical way to think about a data frame is a collection of columns, where each column is a vector.

This section shows two common ways to bring data into your R session.

You can load datasets that already come with R or with an installed package. These are fast and reliable for practice.
You can import data files from your computer, such as CSV or Excel files. These require the correct package, file name, and file path.

We will practice both in this chapter because future chapters will ask you to use built-in package data and imported data files.

Package Datasets
To load package datasets, use the data() function with the name of the dataset and the package it comes from.
📜 The basic SYNTAX: data("dataset_name", package = "package_name")

Base R Datasets
Base R comes with a set of built-in datasets that you can use for practice and learning. These datasets are part of the base R installation and are available without needing to install any additional packages.
🎯 View a list of datasets that are already in R

# ⚡ Type this in your Console to see the available datasets in base R
data(package = "datasets")

🗣 This opens a list of datasets that come from R by default. You can see the name of the dataset and a brief description of it.
These datasets are already available, but you can make their availability more explicit by loading a selected dataset into your Environment with data(). In later chapters, we will often use mtcars from base R.
🎯 Load the mtcars dataset from base R. This is Task 4 of the Practice Space at the end of this chapter.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook to load the mtcars dataset
data("mtcars")

🗣 After running this code, the mtcars dataset is loaded into your R environment.
✅ Look in the Environment pane for mtcars. You can click the object in your environment to view the data. Alternatively, you can run the code View(mtcars). Either method will open a new window in RStudio that displays the data.

🧐 Notice: The mtcars dataset has row names, which are labels stored outside the regular data columns. Row names can be convenient for display, but they do not behave like a regular variable. In most projects, identifiers should be stored as a column instead.

🧶 Test knit.


Curated Datasets
In addition to the base R datasets, there are packages that you can install that provide additional datasets for practice and learning. These datasets are often curated and come with documentation that explains the context and variables in the dataset. One popular package is dslabs, which provides datasets for practice and learning in data science.

# ⚡ Type this in your Console to see what datasets are available from dslabs
data(package = "dslabs")         

🎯 Load the movielens dataset from the dslabs package. This is Task 5 of the Practice Space at the end of this chapter.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook to load the "movielens" dataset
data("movielens", package = "dslabs")

🗣 The movielens dataset from the dslabs package is loaded into the R environment.
✅ You can click the object in your environment to view the data.

🌱 Chapter 8 will teach you how to explore tabular data in more detail.

🧭 If a dataset does not appear, your next step is to check the sequence of your notebook. Code that loads packages and data must come before code that uses those objects.
🧶 Test knit.

These datasets are great for practice, but in real projects, you will often need to import data from external files. The next section shows you how to do that.



External Files
Often, you will need to load data from external files that you have downloaded or created. The most common file formats for data are CSV (.csv) and Excel (.xlsx). To load these files into R, you will need to use functions from the readr and readxl packages, respectively.

Read CSV
Importing a CSV file with read_csv() requires the readr package, which you loaded earlier. If you forget to load readr with library(readr), R will report that it cannot find read_csv().
For the notebook setup used in this chapter, the CSV file is saved in the same folder as the Rmd file. When you Knit, this allows you to use only the file name in the import code.
📜 The basic SYNTAX:
df <- read_csv("file.csv")
🎯 Import the CSV file Values_Transport_dplace.csv into R using read_csv() and store it as dplace_df. This is Task 6 of the Practice Space at the end of this chapter.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook to import the CSV file
dplace_df <- read_csv("Values_Transport_dplace.csv")

🗣 The read_csv() function reads the CSV file and creates dplace_df, a data frame that contains the data from the CSV file.
✅ You can click on dplace_df in your Environment to view the imported data.

🧐 Notice: When loading, R prints an import summary to confirm what it found. The dplace_df data frame contains 185 rows and 7 columns. Delimiter: "," means R detected a comma-separated file. The column specification shows how readr interpreted each column. In this case, chr (3) means 3 character columns: id, name, and sub_case. dbl (4) means 4 numeric columns: domainelement_pk, pk, valueset_pk, and year.

🧶 Test knit.

🧭 If the import does not work, read the first line of the error message and check the most likely problem first.

If the error says the file cannot be opened or does not exist, R cannot find Values_Transport_dplace.csv.

Check the spelling, capitalization, underscores, and .csv ending.
Check that the file is in the same folder as your Rmd file.

If the columns look wrong, the file may not have been read as a comma-separated file.

Make sure you did not open and resave the CSV file in Numbers or Excel.
If you are unsure, delete the file and download a fresh copy.

If the error says could not find function read_csv, the readr package is not loaded.

Run library(readr) in a code chunk before the import code.


🛠 Break Things! Test a common error on purpose. Close and reopen RStudio, then run this line before running library(readr):

dplace_df <- read_csv("Values_Transport_dplace.csv")

You should see an error saying R cannot find the read_csv() function. This does not mean the CSV file is broken. It means the package that contains read_csv() has not been loaded yet.
💡 Tip: Any time you reopen RStudio, run all code chunks to load your packages and data into R again.



Read Excel
Importing an Excel file requires the package readxl that we loaded earlier. If you did not load the readxl package, you will get an error message when you try to use read_excel().
Type read_excel() in your notebook
For the notebook setup used in this chapter, saving the Excel file in the same folder as the Rmd file allows you to use only the file name when you Knit.
df <- read_excel("file.xlsx")
🎯 Import the Excel file car_prices.xlsx into R using read_excel() and store it as car_prices_df. This is Task 7 of the Practice Space at the end of this chapter.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook to import the Excel file
car_prices_df <- read_excel("car_prices.xlsx")


🧐 Notice: Be patient when you load an Excel file. R may take a few seconds to read an Excel file, especially if the file is large, has complex formatting, or if you are importing more than one sheet. Very large Excel files can take longer to import. The limit is usually the computer’s available memory and processing power, not RStudio itself. However, opening a very large dataset in RStudio’s data viewer can slow down the RStudio window a lot.

🗣 The read_excel() function reads the Excel file and creates a data frame called car_prices_df that contains the data from the Excel file. You can click on car_prices_df in your environment to view the imported data.
💡 Tip: If the Excel import fails while the workbook is open in Excel, close the workbook and try the import again.
✅ Look in the Environment pane for car_prices_df. Click the object or run head(car_prices_df) to confirm that the rows and columns look like car price data.
View the data frame by clicking on car_prices_df in your Environment pane or by running View(car_prices_df) in your console.
🧭 If the Excel import does not look right, check three things before asking for help: whether the file is listed in list.files(), whether the file name is spelled exactly as car_prices.xlsx, and whether the workbook has more than one sheet.
🧶 Test knit.


🌳 Multiple Sheets
Excel files can contain multiple sheets. By default, read_excel() reads the first sheet. If your Excel file has multiple sheets, you can specify which sheet to read using the sheet argument. You can specify the sheet by name or by number.

# Optional Example
excel_sheets("car_prices.xlsx")
car_prices_sheet1 <- read_excel("car_prices.xlsx", sheet = 1)

🗣 The excel_sheets() function lists the names of the sheets in the Excel file. The read_excel() function with the sheet argument reads the specified sheet from the Excel file.
🧭 When a workbook has multiple sheets, use excel_sheets() to inspect the available names, then select the sheet you need by number or name. For example, sheet = 1 selects the first sheet, while sheet = "car_prices" selects it by name.
🧶 Test knit.



Create RData file
This task creates an RData file.
🎯 Save the environment objects car_prices_df, dplace_df, movielens, and mtcars into a file called chapter7_practice.RData.
Run this code after car_prices_df, dplace_df, movielens, and mtcars exist in your Environment.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook to save the selected objects in an RData file
save(
  car_prices_df,
  dplace_df,
  movielens,
  mtcars,
  file = "chapter7_practice.RData"
)

🗣 save() writes chapter7_practice.RData in the current working directory. When you Knit the notebook used in this chapter, that directory is the folder containing chapter7_practice.Rmd. After knitting, use list.files() or Finder or File Explorer to confirm that the RData file is there.
🧭 Saving selected objects gives you control over what the RData file restores later. Here, you are preserving the four objects used in this chapter rather than saving everything in the Environment.

title: Chapter 7: Importing Data
text:
Summary
In this chapter, you learned how datasets enter R and why file management is a common reason imports fail. We started by defining tabular data as a table where rows represent observations and columns represent variables. You also learned that imported tabular data is usually stored in a data frame, which is rectangular: every column has the same number of rows, and missing values should appear as NA.
You also learned how the working directory controls where R looks for files. You used getwd() to print the current working directory and list.files() to list the files R can see in that folder. You compared running code in the Console to knitting an Rmd file, where code chunks usually use the Rmd file’s folder as the working directory. To prevent “cannot open file” errors, you practiced saving downloaded data files in the same folder as your R Notebook and checking that the filenames appear in list.files() before importing.
Finally, you practiced the core import workflows introduced in this chapter. You installed packages with install.packages(), verified installation with packageVersion(), and loaded packages each session with library(). You loaded built-in and package datasets with data(), then imported external files with read_csv() for CSV files and read_excel() for Excel files. When something did not work, you used targeted checks for the working directory, file visibility, and loaded packages.
You now have a repeatable import workflow: place the file, check where R is looking, confirm R can see the file, load the right package, import the data, and verify the result. This workflow supports autonomy by helping you use evidence to choose a next step and ask a focused question when you need help.

title: Chapter 7: Importing Data
text:
Chapter Terms
Columns: The vertical fields in a data frame or table. In tidy tabular data, each column usually represents one variable, such as a name, category, measurement, count, or logical value. In R, each column in a data frame is a vector, and all columns must have the same number of rows.
CSV (Comma-Separated Values): A plain-text file (.csv) for rectangular (row-and-column) data where each row is a line and values are separated by commas. Because it’s plain text, CSV is widely compatible across software, but it does not reliably preserve spreadsheet features like formulas, cell formatting, or multiple sheets.
Data Frame: A two-dimensional R object for tabular data, organized as rows and columns. Each column is a vector (or factor) with the same number of rows, columns can have different data types, and the object has class “data.frame”.
Excel (.xlsx): A Microsoft Excel workbook file (.xlsx) that can store one or more worksheets, along with spreadsheet features like formulas and formatting. .xlsx uses the Office Open XML format (the “x” indicates an XML-based file without macros).
File Path: A text “address” that tells the computer (and R) where a file or folder is located. Paths can be absolute (the full location from the start of the file system) or relative (interpreted relative to your current working directory). In R, getwd() shows the current working directory that relative paths are based on, and file.path() helps build paths in an operating-system-safe way.
Graphical User Interface (GUI): A point-and-click interface that lets you interact with software using menus, buttons, and file browsers instead of typing commands. In RStudio, the Import Dataset wizard is a GUI tool that helps you select a file and then outputs the R code (including the file path) needed to reproduce the import, so you can copy that code into your R script.
Package: An installable collection of R code, including functions, documentation, and sometimes datasets, that adds new features beyond base R. Packages are commonly installed from CRAN and then loaded with library() so you can use their tools in your session.
Rows: The horizontal records in a data frame or table. In tidy tabular data, each row usually represents one observation, case, or unit being measured, such as one person, car, state, experiment, or survey response.
Tabular Data: Data arranged in a table (a rectangular structure) where rows represent records/observations and columns represent variables/attributes. This row–column layout is the standard format used by spreadsheets, databases, and data frames.
Working Directory: The folder on your computer that R treats as the default “home base” for the current session. When you read files (e.g., read.csv("data.csv")) or save outputs (e.g., write.csv(df, "results.csv")) using relative paths, R looks in (and writes to) the working directory unless you specify a full path. You can view or change it using Session → Set Working Directory, and you can check it with getwd() or change it with setwd("path/to/folder").

title: Chapter 8: Indexing
text:
Overview
Bracket indexing is one of the main ways you tell R exactly which rows, columns, or values you want to use. Real data analysis rarely uses an entire dataset all at once. Analysts often need to select a few columns, filter rows, extract one column for a summary, correct data-entry problems, or create a new column for later analysis.
In this chapter, you will practice those skills using the field_sightings dataset, a simulated bird-banding dataset where birds are recorded as Tagged or Untagged, and tagged birds can have a band color. The data frame has two columns: Status and Band_Color. In the Practice Space, you will apply the same indexing patterns to Values_Transport_dplace.csv using columns such as id, name, sub_case, and year.
These skills matter because indexing is how you point R at the part of the data you actually mean. If you select the wrong rows, extract the wrong kind of object, or overwrite values without checking first, later analysis can become unreliable. This chapter helps you build the habit of checking what your code returned before moving on.
By the end of Chapter 8, you will be able to:
Watch for the 🧭 autonomy marker throughout this chapter. It identifies places where you inspect evidence, choose an indexing method, or decide what to check next. Use your memos to explain these decisions.

title: Chapter 8: Indexing
text:
Activity Setup
📖 Review: Chapter 7 introduced you to folder organization and how to import data into R. This section will lightly review what you learned, providing you with additional practice. If you need a more detailed refresher on how to import data, start by reviewing Chapter 7 📤 Importing Data.

Create/Save Chapter 8 Notebook
🎯 Create an R Notebook, edit the YAML, and save in Module_4/

Open an R Notebook: Go to File > New File > R Notebook
Keep the YAML header at the top of the notebook and edit it so that it looks like this:

---
title: "Chapter 8 Notes"
author: "[Your Name]"
date: "`r Sys.Date()`"
output: html_notebook
---

Change [Your Name] to your actual name and remove only the default sample content below the YAML header.
Save your R Notebook File > Save As..., choose your course folder, name the file chapter8_notes.

Suggested file structure:
Intro_to_R/
└── Module_4/
    ├── chapter8_notes.Rmd   # Add the guided activity file to your `Module_4/` folder
    ├── chapter7_practice.Rmd
    ├── Values_Transport_dplace.csv
    └── car_prices.xlsx


Downloading Data
You will need two data files for this chapter:

Download Values_Transport_dplace.csv
Download field_sightings.csv

🎯 Click the download link. Do not open the downloaded csv.
🎯 Move the CSV into your Module_4/ folder with your Rmd file.
Intro_to_R/
└── Module_4/
    ├── chapter8_notes.Rmd   
    ├── chapter7_practice.Rmd
    ├── Values_Transport_dplace.csv
    ├── car_prices.xlsx
    └── field_sightings.csv   # Add the CSV file to your `Module_4/` folder
🧭 If your folder has a different structure, that is okay as long as you can explain where your Rmd file is saved and how to address the file path to the data files. The important habit is knowing where your work lives before you try to load data. For novices, it is easiest to place the data files in the same folder as the Rmd file.

Now that you have your R Notebook set up and the data files in place, you are ready to load the data.


Load Data
The field_sightings.csv dataset contains simulated (randomly generated) values. The dataset theme is based on the pretend situation where field biologists observed and recorded a population of species of birds. Bird banding is a scientific method used to track and study individual birds, providing valuable data on their movements, behavior, and population dynamics. In our scenario, most birds observed were “Untagged,” but a small number have been previously captured and marked with colored leg bands, “Tagged”. The color of the bands might provide information about the bird’s history, such as where it was banded or its age.
The simulated data frame field_sightings has two columns:

Status describes whether the sighted bird is “Untagged” (the common case) or “Tagged” (the rare case).
Band_Color records “None” for an untagged bird or one of several possible band colors for a tagged bird.

The dataset also includes a small number of intentionally missing values. These missing values will help demonstrate what happens when a logical condition returns NA.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
# 1) Confirm the CSV is in the same folder as your R Notebook
list.files()

✅ Look in the output from list.files(). Confirm that field_sightings.csv appears exactly as written, including the underscore and .csv ending.
🧭 If field_sightings.csv is not listed, check whether the file is still in Downloads/, whether it was renamed, or whether it was saved in a different folder. Your next move is to make the file visible to R in your Rmd, then run list.files() again.
🎯 Load field_sightings.csv into R using read_csv() and assign it to a variable called field_sightings. Recall that you need to library readr before you can use read_csv().

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
# Load the readr package for reading CSV files
library(readr)

field_sightings <- read_csv("field_sightings.csv")

🗣 This code loads the readr package, uses read_csv() to read the file named field_sightings.csv, and assigns the resulting tibble to an object called field_sightings. It is normal for read_csv() to display a message summarizing the imported rows, columns, and detected column types.
✅ Look in the Environment pane for field_sightings. Then run head(field_sightings) to confirm that the data has two columns, Status and Band_Color.

# ✅ Check
head(field_sightings)

# A tibble: 6 × 2
  Status   Band_Color
  <chr>    <chr>     
1 Untagged None      
2 Untagged None      
3 Untagged None      
4 Untagged None      
5 Untagged None      
6 Untagged None      


✅ Click field_sightings in your Environment pane and confirm that its columns are Status and Band_Color.
As you work, add short memos to your notebook. Use 🗣 Comments to explain your code or output and 🪞 Reflect to record what you understand, what remains uncertain, or what you would check next.
🧶 Test knit. Before you move on, test knit your R Notebook to make sure everything is working. Check that the formatting is working as expected (e.g., headings appear as heading font, code appears in code chunks, and memos are paragraph text)

With your data loaded into the environment, you are ready to start practicing subsetting, extraction, and replacement techniques in R.

title: Chapter 8: Indexing
text:
Subsetting
Subsetting means selecting a smaller part of an object, typically using positions (integers), names (characters), or a logical mask (TRUE/FALSE). In base R, this is done using the single square bracket operator [ ([ ]).
The structure returned by [ ] depends on the object being indexed and the way the index is written. A subset of a vector is still a vector. In this chapter, read_csv() creates a tibble, and [ ] keeps a one-column selection as a one-column tibble. When you need the values inside one column as a vector, use an extraction operator such as [[ ]] or $. Data analysts use subsetting when filtering rows, selecting columns to keep, slicing a range, or pulling a rectangular block from a data frame.

📍 Positional Indexing
Positional indexing is the most basic form of indexing in R, where you use numeric positions to select elements from a vector or data frame.
💡 Tip: Positions start at 1 in R. This is different from other coding languages like Python, which starts indexing values at 0.

Vector
In Chapter 3, you practiced using the indexing operator with positional indexing to extract elements from vectors. Let’s review that briefly before we move on to data frames.
You learned that the basic pattern for positional indexing is x[i], where x is the vector and i is the index (or indices) of the elements you want to select. An index identifies a position in an object.
🎯 Practice using [ ] with positional indexing on vectors.

# 📖 Review
z <- c(10, 20, 30, 40, 50) # create a vector

# ✅  Check
print(z)

[1] 10 20 30 40 50



# 📖 Review
z[1]       

[1] 10


🗣 The first element by position is 10.

# 📖 Review
z[3]      

[1] 30


🗣 The third element by position is 30.

# 📖 Review
z[2:4]     

[1] 20 30 40


🗣 The second, third and fourth elements by position are 20, 30, and 40.


Data Frame
The indexing operator ([ ]) is used to select or replace parts of many kinds of objects, not just vectors. For data frames, the common form is df[rows, cols] or x[i, j] where i is the row index, j is the column index. If you leave one side blank, the output includes all.
Rows and columns are coordinates:

df[1:5, ] results in the first five rows, all columns
df[ , 1:3] shows all rows, first three columns
df[1, 2] selects the first row and second column. For a tibble such as field_sightings, the result remains a one-row, one-column tibble.

Let’s see this in practice with our field_sightings data frame.
🎯 Print the first six rows of the field_sightings data frame using the indexing operator.
🧭 Before running a bracket-indexing line below, pause and ask: “How do I know that this is choosing rows?”

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
field_sightings[1:6, ]  

# A tibble: 6 × 2
  Status   Band_Color
  <chr>    <chr>     
1 Untagged None      
2 Untagged None      
3 Untagged None      
4 Untagged None      
5 Untagged None      
6 Untagged None      


💡 Tip: I remember bracket indexing by watching the comma. In df[rows, columns], the comma divides the row instruction from the column instruction. The left side answers “which rows?” The right side answers “which columns?” In df[rows, cols], the comma is the divider.
✅ Check that the output has 6 rows and both columns. The blank space after the comma means “keep all columns.”
🗣 This shows the first six rows of field_sightings while keeping all columns.


head() Function Comparison
There is a function called head() that basically does the same thing as field_sightings[1:6, ] but is more concise and easier to read.
📜 The SYNTAX:
head(x, n = 6L)
If you don’t specify n, it defaults to 6, which means it will show the first 6 rows of the data frame. You can change this number to show more or fewer rows.
🎯 Print the first three rows of the field_sightings data frame using the head() function to check that the dataset loaded correctly.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
head(field_sightings, n = 3)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  Status   Band_Color
  <chr>    <chr>     
1 Untagged None      
2 Untagged None      
3 Untagged None      


✅ Confirm that the output shows exactly 3 rows and the same column names as the full data frame.
🗣 head() is commonly used to get a quick orientation of the dataset after loading.
head() does not do arbitrary extraction or subsetting. head() is a function that provides a convenient way to view the first few rows of a data frame.
🧭 Use head() when you want a quick look at the beginning of a dataset. Use bracket indexing when you need to select specific rows, columns, or conditions.
🧶 Test knit.

Bracket indexing allows for flexible and specific subsetting of the data frame based on row and column indices. [ works on almost everything and supports rich indexing and is commonly used as part of an algorithm. You will use [ when you need subsetting by columns, conditions, and arbitrary rows when you are writing analysis code.



🏷 Names Indexing
You can also use names indexing (also referred to as character indexing) to select columns by their names instead of their positions. This often makes more readable code and is less error-prone, especially when the order of columns might change or when you have many columns.

Vector
In Chapter 3, you created the nerdy_palette vector and then used names indexing to return the hexadecimal color code.

# 📖 Review
# Create nerdy_palette
nerdy_palette <- c(
  "Octarine"      = "#7F00FF",
  "TARDIS Blue"   = "#003B6F",
  "Rebeccapurple" = "#663399",
  "Hooloovoo"     = "#4F97A3",
  "Cosmic Latte"  = "#FFF8E7",
  "Vantablack"    = "#000000",
  "Matrix Green"  = "#03A062",
  "Source Engine Magenta" = "#FF00FF",
  "Command Red"   = "#CC0000",
  "Impossible Green" = "#4D9E68"
  )

# ✅ Use names indexing to return the hex code for Octarine
nerdy_palette["Octarine"]

 Octarine 
"#7F00FF" 


🗣 The output shows the hexadecimal color code for “Octarine” retrieved from the nerdy_palette vector using its name.


Data Frame
A common use of names indexing is to select a column by its name.
🎯 Use names indexing to return the band colors in the field_sightings data frame.
Methods A–C compare ways to select one column by name.
Method A
📜 The SYNTAX: x[i]

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
field_sightings["Band_Color"]         # 1-column DATA FRAME

✅ Check the output structure.
🗣 A one-column tibble is printed showing all row values in the Band_Color column of the field_sightings tibble. It is a subset that keeps the rectangular tibble structure.
Method B
📜 The SYNTAX: x[[i]]

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
# Example B
field_sightings[["Band_Color"]]   # column VECTOR

✅ Check the output structure.
🗣 A vector is printed showing all values from the Band_Color column of the field_sightings tibble. This is extraction: it returns the column values rather than a one-column tibble.
Method C
📜 The SYNTAX: x[i, j, drop = FALSE]

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
# Example C
field_sightings[, "Band_Color", drop = FALSE]    # 1-column TIBBLE

✅ Check the output structure.
🗣 A one-column tibble is printed showing all row values in the Band_Color column of the field_sightings tibble. The explicit drop = FALSE instruction says to keep the rectangular structure.

⚠️ Common Pain Point: Students often forget to put the column name in quotes when using names indexing. If you forget the quotes, R will look for an object named Band_Color in your environment and return an error if it doesn’t find one. Always remember to put column names in quotes when using names indexing with [ ].

🧭 Choose a method based on the kind of output you need next. If you need a smaller data frame, keep the data-frame structure. If you need the values inside one column, extract the column as a vector.
🧶 Test knit.

So far, you’ve learned about positional indexing and names indexing. Both of these methods rely on you knowing the positions or names of the elements you want to subset. But what if you want to subset based on a condition, like keeping only rows where Status is “Tagged”? This is where logical mask indexing comes in.



🔍 Logical Mask Indexing
A logical mask is the logical vector you use to index.

Vector
In Chapter 4, you practiced logical indexing with a vector.
🎯 Create a new vector called smaller that contains only values in number_list that are less than or equal to 20.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
# Create the sample vector
number_list <- c(10, 25, 5, 30, 15, 40)

# ✅  Check
print(number_list)

[1] 10 25  5 30 15 40


🗣 The number_list vector contains the values 10, 25, 5, 30, 15, and 40.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
# Example 1
# Step 1: create the logical "mask"
mask <- number_list <= 20

# ✅  Check
print(mask)

[1]  TRUE FALSE  TRUE FALSE  TRUE FALSE


✅ Check that mask has the same number of values as number_list. Each value should be TRUE or FALSE, depending on whether the matching number is less than or equal to 20.
🗣 This prints the mask. The mask itself is not a subset of the original vector. The logical vector indicates which values in number_list are less than or equal to 20.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
# Example 1
# Step 2: use the logical vector inside [ ]
smaller <- number_list[mask]

# ✅  Check
print(smaller)

[1] 10  5 15


✅ Check that smaller contains only the values from number_list where the mask was TRUE: 10, 5, and 15.
🗣 This keeps only the values where the condition is TRUE (10, 5, 15).
You can also pass the mask directly into the indexing operator without storing it in a variable first.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
# Example 2
smaller <- number_list[number_list <= 20]

🗣 Both example 1 and example 2 are conditional subsetting or filtering by using a logical condition. These examples use the less than or equal to (<=) relational operator.
[ ] uses it as a filter. Logical indexing is a form of indexing in R where you use a logical vector (a “mask” of TRUE/FALSE values) to select elements from a vector or rows from a data frame.
R keeps the values where the mask is TRUE and drops the values where the mask is FALSE.
🧶 Test knit.

📖 Review: Chapter 3 introduced comparison operators.



Operator
Meaning
Example




>
greater than
mpg > 20


<
less than
mpg < 15


==
equal to
am == 1


>=
greater or equal
mpg >= 25


<=
less or equal
mpg <= 15


!
not
!(gear %in% c(3,4))


!=
not equal to
gear != 4




🧭 Storing the mask first (example 1) is useful when you want to inspect or reuse the logic. Putting the condition directly inside [ ] (example 2) is useful when the condition is short and easy to read. Both are valid.
Let’s see this in action in a dataframe.


Data Frame
Logical mask indexing works the same way for data frames, except that the logical mask usually goes in the rows position of df[rows, cols].
The mask can be TRUE/FALSE/NA for each row. When you use the mask in df[mask, ], R keeps rows where the mask is TRUE. If the mask contains NA, those unknown positions can also appear in the result, which can make the subset larger than the number of definite TRUE values.
🎯 Use a logical mask with [ ] to subset rows based on whether the bird is tagged, then inspect how missing values affect the result.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
# Step 1: create the logical mask (one TRUE/FALSE/NA per row)
mask_tagged <- field_sightings[["Status"]] == "Tagged"

🗣 The == is the equal to comparison operator that checks if the value in the Status column is equal to “Tagged”. A single = is used for assigning values inside some function calls (like na.rm = TRUE) and naming arguments. It is not used to test equality.
✅ Check the first few values with head(mask_tagged). You should see a logical vector containing TRUE, FALSE, and possibly NA.

# ✅  Check
head(mask_tagged)

[1] FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE


🗣 This prints a logical vector the same length as the number of rows in field_sightings. Each TRUE means the corresponding row has Status == "Tagged", each FALSE means it does not, and each NA means the status is unknown.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
# Step 2: use the logical mask inside [ ] to subset rows
tagged_only <- field_sightings[mask_tagged, ]

# Alternative: pass the logical mask directly into [ ]
# tagged_only <- field_sightings[field_sightings[["Status"]] == "Tagged", ]

✅ Look at the Status column in the first few rows of tagged_only. You should mostly see “Tagged”, but if the mask contained NA, you may also see rows with missing values.

# ✅  Check
head(tagged_only)

# A tibble: 6 × 2
  Status Band_Color
  <chr>  <chr>     
1 Tagged Orange    
2 Tagged Silver    
3 Tagged Green     
4 Tagged Black     
5 Tagged Silver    
6 Tagged Blue      


🗣 This subsets the data frame using the logical mask. Rows where the mask is TRUE are retained. Because the mask also contains NA, unknown rows appear in the result as rows of missing values.
✅ Compare the three counts. nrow(field_sightings) tells you the size of the original data frame. nrow(tagged_only) tells you how many rows were returned by the subset. sum(mask_tagged, na.rm = TRUE) tells you how many rows were definitely TRUE.

# ✅  Check
nrow(field_sightings)            # how many rows in the original data frame?

[1] 4470

nrow(tagged_only)                # how many rows were returned?

[1] 325

sum(mask_tagged, na.rm= TRUE)    # how many TRUE values in the mask?

[1] 300


🗣 The result contains 300 confirmed Tagged rows plus 25 rows produced by the NA positions in the mask. We use na.rm = TRUE to count only the confirmed TRUE values. We can tell the mask contains NA values because nrow(tagged_only) (325) is larger than sum(mask_tagged, na.rm = TRUE) (300).
🧶 Test knit.

Logical mask indexing is a powerful way to subset data frames based on conditions, but missing values can make the results harder to interpret. When we compute mask_tagged <- field_sightings[["Status"]] == "Tagged", any row where Status is NA produces NA because NA == "Tagged" is unknown. That’s missing value propagation! This is where missing values carry through comparisons as NA.
When we then subset with tagged_only <- field_sightings[mask_tagged, ], R keeps rows where the mask is TRUE, but it does not treat NA as FALSE. Rows with NA in the mask can appear in the subset rows, which is why tagged_only has 325 rows even though there are only 300 TRUE values in the mask.


which() Function Helper
The function which() is a subsetting helper that turns a logical mask into row indices. Using which() is one strategy for handling potential NA values in a logical test. which() returns the positions that are TRUE and omits positions that are FALSE or NA.
🎯 Use which() to subset the field_sightings data frame to keep only rows where the bird is tagged, while safely handling any potential NA values in the “Status” column.
You saw the function which() in Chapter 6. This function converts TRUE positions into numeric indices.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook

# Pass logic through which() to get the row indices where Status is "Tagged"
row_idx_tagged <- which(field_sightings[["Status"]] == "Tagged")

## Alternative: Create mask_tagged then pass it to which() to get row indices
# mask_tagged <- field_sightings[["Status"]] == "Tagged"
# row_idx_tagged <- which(mask_tagged)

✅ Check head(row_idx_tagged) to confirm that which() returned row numbers, not TRUE/FALSE values.

# ✅  Check
head(row_idx_tagged)

[1] 18 22 31 41 50 66



# Use the row indices to subset the data frame by rows that are tagged
tagged_only <- field_sightings[row_idx_tagged, ]

✅ Compare nrow(tagged_only) to length(row_idx_tagged). These should match because row_idx_tagged contains the exact row positions used to create tagged_only.

# ✅  Check
nrow(tagged_only) 

[1] 300

length(row_idx_tagged)

[1] 300


🗣 I used which() because I wanted only confirmed Tagged rows. The subset has 300 rows, matching the number of TRUE positions in the mask. The 25 unknown statuses were omitted.
🧭 Use a plain logical mask when the condition is simple and you have already checked how missing values behave. Use which() when you want row positions and want to avoid carrying NA values into the subset.
🧶 Test knit.

In conclusion, subsetting ([ ]) returns a piece of the original object, often preserving structure. When you need a smaller data frame, subset. If you need values within another function, you’ll need to extract. In the next section, you will learn how extraction returns one component’s contents.

title: Chapter 8: Indexing
text:
Extraction
Extraction means pulling out a single component. When you want the column values themselves as a vector, operators [[ ]] and $ are the clearest extraction approach. Extraction pulls out a single component (one column or one list element) so you can use it inside a function or calculation. Data analysts use extracted objects in a specific part of more complex code that creates a plot or summary.

[[ Operator
There is an operator called the double square bracket operator ([[ ]]). [ is the general subsetting operator. [[ ]] extracts exactly one component. With a tibble, [ keeps a one-column selection as a tibble, while [[ ]] pulls out that column’s values as a vector.







Operator
Meaning




[ ]
Subsetting operator. Selects one or more elements, rows, or columns. With a tibble, a one-column selection remains a tibble.


[[ ]]
Extraction operator. Returns one component, such as a column vector, so its values can be passed into a function.



🎯 Use the [[ operator to extract the “Band_Color” column from the field_sightings data frame and then use it inside the function unique()
📜 The SYNTAX: x[[i]]
Step 1
Extract a column as a vector

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
field_sightings[["Band_Color"]]   # the column VECTOR


🧐 Notice: This output is long. Use the code chunk option results = 'hide' to run the code while hiding its printed output in your HTML report. The Code Chunk Options section explains how.

✅ Check that the output is a vector of values, not a 1-column data frame. You should see the band color values printed directly.
🗣 The result is an extraction from one column and returns a vector, values only.
Step 2
Use the extracted vector inside the function unique()

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
unique(field_sightings[["Band_Color"]])

 [1] "None"   "Orange" "Silver" "Green"  "Black"  NA       "Blue"   "White" 
 [9] "Red"    "Yellow"


✅ Check that unique() returns each band color only once. This confirms that [[ ]] extracted the column values you wanted to inspect.
🗣 This shows the unique band colors in the field_sightings data frame. Extracting the column with [[ ]] gives unique() the values from that column.
🧭 If a function needs the values inside one column, extraction is usually the better move. Ask yourself: “Does the next function need a data frame, or does it need the column values themselves?”
🧶 Test knit.



$ Operator
There is another operator called the dollar sign operator ($) that is used to extract columns from a data frame by name. It is a convenient shorthand for selecting a single column by name when you type the name literally.
📜 The SYNTAX:
dataframe$column_name
🎯 Extract the Band_Color column using $.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
field_sightings$Band_Color

✅ Check that $ returns the same kind of vector output as field_sightings[["Band_Color"]].
🗣 A vector is printed showing all element values from the column Band_Color from the field_sightings data frame. It is an extraction from one column and returns a vector, values only.
You will likely use the $ operator often. The $ operator is more concise and easier to read for common use cases. However, it only works for selecting one column at a time and can’t use an assigned variable stored in the environment.
If we try to use a variable to specify the column name with the $ operator, it will not work because $ does not evaluate the variable name. [[ ]] can use a variable and is safer in programs.
🎯 Use a stored object name to specify the column name and try to extract the column using both [[ and $ operators.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
# Example 1
col_name <- "Band_Color"
field_sightings[[col_name]]   # ✅ works

🗣 The [[ operator allows you to use a variable name from your environment to specify the column name, which is why it works in this case. The result is an extraction from one column and returns a vector, values only.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
# Example 2
col_name <- "Band_Color"
field_sightings$col_name      # ❌ looks for a column literally named "col_name"

Warning: Unknown or uninitialised column: `col_name`.


NULL


✅ Check the output. Because there is no column literally named col_name, the tibble should display a warning about an unknown column and return NULL.
🗣 The $ operator looks for a column literally named col_name. The warning and NULL result are expected evidence that the requested column does not exist.
🧭 This is a method-choice decision. Use $ when you are typing the column name directly. Use [[ ]] when the column name is stored in an object. If your code uses a stored column name and returns NULL, check whether you used $ when you needed [[ ]].
🧶 Test knit.

So far, you’ve learned two different moves:

Subset: field_sightings["Band_Color"] (data frame)
Extract: field_sightings[["Band_Color"]] or field_sightings$Band_Color (values)

Next, we’ll learn how to change values inside an existing object using replacement methods.

title: Chapter 8: Indexing
text:
Subassignment (replacement)
Subassignment means replacing part of an object (vector, matrix, data frame, list, etc.) with new values using indexing. It is an umbrella term for assigning into part of an object using an index on the left of <-.
In this chapter, you’ll use three core replacement patterns for data frames:

Use x[i, j] <- value to change specific rows and columns.
Use x[[...]] <- value to replace/add one column (works when the column name is stored in a variable).
Use x$name <- value to replace/add one column (when the column name is typed literally).

👉 Indexing on the left of <- edits the object you assign into.

Overwrite with x[i, j] <- value
Overwrite is an informal type of replacement where you change existing values.
📜 The SYNTAX:
x[i, j] <- value

🧐 Notice: Indexing is located on the left side of an assignment operator (<-) to change specific values in a data frame.

What if all the tagged birds in the field_sightings data frame were raised as part of a breeding program and then reintroduced into an area where the species no longer existed? This means all the untagged birds were hatched in the wild. Suppose we decide to rename the element value "Untagged" to "Wild Hatch" in the Status column to communicate this information more clearly.
🎯 Replace "Untagged" with "Wild Hatch" in Status.
Step 1
Make a copy of the data frame.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
reintroduction <- field_sightings          # copy

✅ Check the Environment pane. You should now see both field_sightings and reintroduction.
🧭 Making a copy is a protective habit. It gives you the freedom to experiment because the original data frame is still available for comparison if your replacement code does something unexpected.
🗣 We will overwrite values using the copy dataframe, reintroduction.
Step 2
Get row indices with which() to identify the rows where Status is “Untagged”. which() returns the row positions where the test is TRUE and ignores positions where the test is FALSE or NA. Use the dataframe that you want to overwrite values in, not the original data frame.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
indices_untagged <- which(reintroduction[["Status"]] == "Untagged")

✅ Run head(indices_untagged) to confirm that which() returned row numbers. These are the row positions where Status was “Untagged”.

# ✅  Check
head(indices_untagged)

[1] 1 2 3 4 5 6


Step 3
Overwrite using df[rows, "col"] <- value

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
reintroduction[indices_untagged, "Status"] <- "Wild Hatch"

Step 4
✅ Verify that the values have been changed.
Compare the two outputs. reintroduction should include “Wild Hatch”. The original field_sightings should still include “Untagged”.

# ✅  Check
unique(reintroduction[["Status"]])       # modified data frame

[1] "Wild Hatch" "Tagged"     NA          

unique(field_sightings[["Status"]])      # original data frame

[1] "Untagged" "Tagged"   NA        


🗣 The copy now contains “Wild Hatch”, while the original still contains “Untagged”. These checks show that I changed the intended values and preserved the original data.
🧶 Test knit.



Insertion
Insertion is an informal type of replacement where you add something new (most commonly a new column).
x[[...]] <- value and x$name <- value replace (or create) one component. For data frames, that’s typically a single column.
Suppose we decide to add a new column called Tag_Flag that indicates whether the bird is tagged. It is common to use binary columns to create figures or run analyses. We want to set the value to 1 for confirmed Tagged birds, 0 for confirmed Untagged birds, and NA when Status is missing.

[[ Method
🎯 Add a new column (a flag) using a column name stored in a variable.
Step 1
Make a copy of the data frame.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
reintroduction2 <- field_sightings

✅ Check that reintroduction2 appears in the Environment pane. This is the copy you will modify.
Step 2
Store the new name of your column in a variable.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
new_col <- "Tag_Flag"

✅ Check that new_col contains the text “Tag_Flag”. This object stores the new column name.
Step 3
Add the new column using [[ ]] <-

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
# Start with NA because some Status values are missing
reintroduction2[[new_col]] <- NA_integer_    # <- Uses [[]]

# Assign 0 to confirmed Untagged birds and 1 to confirmed Tagged birds
idx_untagged <- which(reintroduction2[["Status"]] == "Untagged")
idx_tagged <- which(reintroduction2[["Status"]] == "Tagged")
reintroduction2[idx_untagged, new_col] <- 0
reintroduction2[idx_tagged, new_col] <- 1

Step 4
✅ Verify that the new column has been added and values are correct.
Run names(reintroduction2) and confirm that Tag_Flag appears as a new column name.

# ✅  Check
names(reintroduction2)

[1] "Status"     "Band_Color" "Tag_Flag"  

table(reintroduction2[["Tag_Flag"]], useNA = "always")


   0    1 <NA> 
4145  300   25 


✅ Confirm that the table reports 4,145 values of 0, 300 values of 1, and 25 NA values.

title: Chapter 8: Indexing
text:
Code Chunk Options
You probably noticed that some code chunk examples in this chapter resulted in long vector outputs. These can become difficult to read and navigate. You might find them particularly annoying when reviewing your HTML report. This final section explains how to manage long outputs in your R Notebook.
To make your R Notebook more readable, you can use the results = 'hide' option in your code chunks to hide the output of certain chunks, especially those that produce long outputs.
Alternatively, you can use eval = FALSE to prevent the code from running at all, which is useful for code that is meant to be illustrative rather than executed, such as when there is an error that you want to discuss without actually running the code.
Inspect messages and warnings before deciding to hide them. If they explain an unresolved problem, keep them visible and record what you checked in a memo. The example that hides messages and warnings below uses code you have already checked.
Below are some examples of how to use these options in your R Notebook. Try out the code chunk settings in your notebook to see how they work!
```{r, echo=TRUE, results='hide'}
# Show code, hide long output
field_sightings[['Band_Color']]
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Run checked code; hide code/messages/warnings
head(field_sightings)
```

```{r, eval=FALSE, echo=TRUE}
# Show code, but do not run it
field_sightings$Band_Color
```
🎯 Experiment with these options in your R Notebook to find the best way to manage long outputs above to make your notes and practice reports more readable. Knit your notebook to HTML to see how it looks, then adjust the options and other formatting and re-knit to make sure your report is professional and ready to share with your research collaborators.
✅ Knit your notebook and look at the HTML output. Confirm whether the code, output, messages, and warnings appear or are hidden the way you intended.
🧭 Code chunk options are report-design decisions. Use them to make your notebook easier to read, not to hide evidence that your code failed. If a warning or message helps explain what happened, keep it visible or memo it.

title: Chapter 8: Indexing
text:
Summary
In Chapter 8, you learned how to use base R indexing to select, extract, and modify parts of a data frame. These skills are useful because most analysis does not use every row and every column at the same time. You need to be able to point R at the exact part of the data you want and check that R returned what you intended.
You practiced subsetting with [ ] using the df[rows, cols] pattern. You selected rows and columns by position, selected columns by name, and used logical masks to keep rows that met a condition. You also learned that the output can change depending on how you index. Some code returns a data frame, while other code returns a vector, and that difference matters for what you can do next.
You also practiced extraction with [[ ]] and $. Extraction pulls out one column as a vector, which is useful when you want to pass the column values into functions such as unique() or table(). You learned that [[ ]] is safer when the column name is stored in an object, while $ is convenient when you type the column name directly.
Logical masks introduced an important warning about missing values. When a comparison involves NA, the result can also be NA. That means a logical mask can contain TRUE, FALSE, and NA, which can make subsetting results harder to interpret. You practiced using which() to convert TRUE values into row positions and avoid carrying unknown values into the subset.
Finally, you practiced subassignment by making a copy of a data frame, finding row positions with which(), and overwriting selected values. You also practiced adding a new column. These are important data-cleaning skills because real datasets often need corrections or new variables before they are ready for analysis.
The main habit to carry forward is this: after indexing, extracting, or modifying data, verify what changed. Check the dimensions, names, object type, values, or summary output before moving on. In later chapters, you will extend this work by filtering with more complex conditions using &, |, and %in%.

title: Chapter 8: Indexing
text:
Chapter Terms
Column index: The index used to select columns in a data frame or matrix (the second slot inside brackets: x[, j]).
Conditional Subsetting (Logical Subsetting): Filtering an object by using a logical condition inside [ ] (e.g., df[df$cyl != 4, ]), where TRUE keeps an element/row and FALSE drops it. This contrasts with negative indexing, which excludes by position rather than by a condition.
Dollar Sign Operator ($): An extraction (and replacement) operator used to access one named component, such as a data frame column (df$col) or a list element (lst$name). $ uses the name typed after it rather than a column name stored in a variable. If the name does not exist, it returns NULL. The tibbles used in this chapter also display an unknown-column warning.
Double Square Bracket Operator ([[): An extraction operator used to pull out one single element from a list (or one column from a data frame) and return the element itself, not a same-type subset. Unlike [, which can return multiple elements and preserves the container type, [[ is for “give me the one thing inside” (e.g., a vector inside a dataframe).
Equal To (==): A relational operator that tests equality and returns TRUE where values are equal and FALSE where they are not (element-by-element for vectors).
Extraction: Retrieving a single component from an object, such as one list element or one data-frame column, so you get the component’s contents (often a vector). Extraction is commonly done with [[ ]] (extract one element by position or name) or $ (extract one column by name).
Indexing Operator: The single square bracket operator [ ] selects or replaces parts of an object in R. For a vector, x[i] selects values by position, name, or logical condition. For a data frame, df[rows, cols] selects rows and columns. The double square bracket operator [[ ]] extracts one component and has its own definition above.
Insertion: A common type of subassignment where you add something new to an object, most often a new column in a data frame. Example: df[["Tag_Flag"]] <- 0 (creates the column if it doesn’t exist yet).
Less Than or Equal To (<=): A relational operator that returns TRUE where the left side is less than or equal to the right side, and FALSE otherwise.
Logical Indexing: Indexing a vector using a logical vector of TRUE/FALSE values (for example, x[x > 0]) so R keeps the elements where the index is TRUE and drops those where it is FALSE. If the logical index is a different length, R may recycle it, which can lead to surprising results.
Logical Mask: A logical vector used inside the single square bracket operator [ to filter another object. Each TRUE marks a value or row to keep, and each FALSE marks a value or row to leave out; for the cleanest results, the mask should line up element-by-element with the object being filtered. For example, number_list <= 20 creates a logical mask, and number_list[mask] uses that mask to keep only the matching values.
Missing Value Propagation: R’s behavior where an NA (unknown value) “carries through” computations and comparisons. If an operation can’t be determined because of missing data, the result is often NA (unknown) instead of TRUE or FALSE. For example, NA == "Tagged" returns NA. If you use a logical mask that contains NA values for subsetting (e.g., x[mask] or df[mask, ]), R does not treat NA as FALSE, so the subset may include NA values (or NA rows), which can change counts and results.
Names Indexing: Selecting parts of an object using character strings that match element or column names. Examples: x[c("Octarine", "TARDIS Blue")] selects named vector elements, and df[, c("id", "year")] selects data frame columns. A name that does not exist returns NA when subsetting a named vector, but selecting a missing data frame column produces an error.
Overwrite: A common type of subassignment where you change existing values (you replace what is already there). Example: df[rows, "Status"] <- "Wild Hatch".
Positional Indexing: Indexing a vector using numeric positions (for example, x[1] for the first element or x[c(1, 3)] for the first and third). Positions are based on the current order of the vector.
Row index: The index used to select rows in a data frame or matrix (the first slot inside brackets: x[i, ]).
Subassignment: Replacing part of an object by putting an index on the left side of <-. R changes only the indexed part of the object. Examples: x[i] <- value, df[rows, "col"] <- value, df[[col]] <- value, df$col <- value.
Subsetting: Selecting a smaller piece of an R object using indices (positions, names, or a logical mask). With data frames, subsetting most commonly uses [ in the form df[rows, cols] and typically preserves the object’s structure (e.g., you still get a data frame when you subset rows and columns).

title: Open-mindedness
text:
Open-mindedness while learning R
Learning R introduces you to different ways of approaching the same task. You may encounter an unfamiliar method, hear another explanation, or get a result that challenges what you expected. These moments invite you to examine another possibility and consider what you can learn from it.
Baehr (2022) describes intellectual open-mindedness as a willingness and ability to step outside a familiar way of thinking long enough to give another perspective fair consideration. This requires trying to understand the alternative on its own terms. Considering another perspective can help you recognize an assumption, correct a misunderstanding, or develop a fuller understanding of an idea.
King (2021) explains that open-mindedness is compatible with confidence in a well-supported belief. You can take another idea seriously while continuing to hold your own view. Evidence may give you a reason to revise your thinking, or it may support your original understanding. Open-mindedness and intellectual firmness work together: consider alternatives carefully and retain conclusions that remain well supported.
Open-mindedness is the learning skill theme for this module. While learning R, you will practice considering different interpretations, methods, and workflows. Your goal is to understand the possibilities and use evidence to decide what to keep or revise.
An unexpected result is an opportunity to reconsider your first interpretation. Suppose a filter returns rows you did not intend to include. Read the data question again, explain the code in words, and examine how R evaluates the conditions. You may discover that the code expresses a different rule from the one you had in mind.
You will also encounter different ways to accomplish similar tasks. A filter might use separate logical vectors or one combined expression. Base R brackets and dplyr functions can often select the same data. Give an unfamiliar approach enough attention to understand how it works. Compare the results, then consider which version makes the reasoning easier to follow.
New tools offer opportunities to examine your workflow from another perspective. Git and GitHub introduce version control, and Quarto provides another way to combine code, output, and written explanation. As you learn these tools, identify what remains familiar, what changes, and how the new approach supports your work.
Another person may also understand your code differently from how you intended it. Listening to their explanation can help you notice an ambiguous condition or a confusing layout. Use their perspective to examine your work, and check any suggested changes before adopting them.

title: Open-mindedness
section: How open-mindedness appears in this book
text:
How open-mindedness appears in this book
The thinking-face emoji 🤔 marks opportunities to consider another way of understanding or approaching your work.
It may invite you to:

examine an interpretation that differs from your first reading,
understand another way to write the same filtering rule,
reconsider an assumption when the output gives you a reason,
give an unfamiliar tool or workflow a fair trial,
or consider how another reader might understand your code.

When you see 🤔, pause long enough to understand the alternative. Use the task’s goal and the available evidence to decide whether to retain your original approach or revise it.
The ✅ marker directs you to check code or output. The 🤔 marker asks you to consider what another interpretation or approach might help you understand.
Use your memos to make this thinking visible. A 🗣 Comment can explain how two expressions differ or what their results show. A 🪞 Reflect memo can describe an assumption you reconsidered, what you learned from another approach, or why you retained your original understanding. Add a 👀 Cite memo when a human or digital resource contributes to your work.

text:
Overview
In this guided activity, you will connect GitHub, Git, and RStudio so they can work together. You will create a small GitHub repository, clone it into RStudio as a project, make changes locally, commit those changes, push them to GitHub, and practice pulling before you work.
